entry.title: How to Sprinkle in Some Red This Fall
entry.summary: Start with a pop of color — or go monochromatic.
entry.content:
Last year, I posted a carousel of outfits to Instagram that included a picture of me wearing a red sweater vest with a black blazer and another one of me wearing a red Agnès B. snap cardigan under a dark car coat. One of my friends, a former fashion sales executive, commented, “Hint of red should be your signature,” and I thought that was actually really good advice. Like many New Yorkers, I wear a lot of dark clothing in the cooler months, and incorporating red accents — with a sock or a scarf or pants — is an easy way to liven up the look. Here are some easy ways to add a bit of color to your wardrobe

A flash of red peeking out from under a pant hem is always a good look. I also love the idea of red tights under a skirt.

Whether you’re all in on the triangle scarf — a.k.a. “scrap of cashmere” — trend or not, the allure of draping a tomato-colored swath of your preferred natural fiber is undeniable.

A red hat could provide a nice little bit of punctuation to an outfit.

I love the look of a red sweater in the fall, especially when paired with brown pants. Some might even say that red is a neutral. Start with a sweater vest if a full-on knit feels like too much of a commitment. (My red vest is from Dôen and is now sold out, but I found some others that have the same effect.) Strategist writer Brenley Goertzen, who recently told us about some of her favorite polo sweaters, gave us a good tip: Quince’s version of red is spot-on.

Complete an entire outfit with red pants, just like Strategist updates coordinator Najwa Jamal, who went on a hunt for the perfect pair.

My high-vamp red ballet flats have been stealing the show in a couple of recent try-on stories I’ve done (for Eileen Fisher and Uniqlo). They are Mansur Gavriel’s Dream Ballerinas in “poppy” and are made of a laminated suede that has held up beautifully over the three years I’ve had them. They are currently sold out, though you can find a pair or two, depending on size, here. Below are some other solid options.

entry.title: $55 UGGs and 30 Percent Off Abercrombie Kids: The Week’s Best Kids’ Deals
entry.summary: Including gift-worthy toys, Strategist-vetted baby gear, and cozy the North Face gloves.
entry.content:
Black Friday is still about three weeks away, but the early Black Friday sales have already begun. There are markdowns at Nordstrom on cozy winter accessories like UGG slip-ons and the North Face gloves, and kids’ jewelry brand Pierced is offering 25 percent off sitewide on tons of huggies, hoops, and studs right now. I also sniffed out discounts on some classic toys, including a Bop It! and wooden supermarket set, and some Strategist-tested baby gear such as carriers and monitors.

If you want to stay updated on all things kid- and sale- (and kids’-sale-) related, I strongly suggest you sign up for the (free!) Strategist Deal Freaks Daily newsletter to have all of the day’s best discounts sent straight to your inbox. You can also subscribe to the The Strategist Kids’ Department to receive a weekly digest of our babies-and-kids coverage.

A very useful game to have on hand if the kids have the jitters. “It has the sort of feel of a screen or a video game without being one,” says New York deputy editor Alexis Swerdloff.

A plastic-free version of the popular Rush Hour game with solid beechwood cars designed in a vibrant mid-century style.

This wooden supermarket set is a fun alternative to a play kitchen that comes recommended by pediatric physical therapist KC Rickerd. It’s especially good for children to play with together in groups.

This three-dimensional, Tetris-esque brainteaser game prompts kids to place one of the 12 shapes in a specific spot on the board and fit the rest into the surrounding grid. It’s very portable, so it’s great for travel or keeping kids busy at restaurants and would make a nice stocking stuffer too.

This kit comes with everything you need to decorate ten rocks, including glow-in-the-dark and metallic paint.

Senior writer Liza Corsillo recommended Hugg-a-Planet on our guide to the best gifts for 4-year-olds. “Its planet-shaped pillows are made with cotton covers and the designs are colorful yet tasteful enough to display on an adult’s couch,” she writes. “Best of all, they are wonderful conversation starters for curious children.”

One of our favorite books to gift to little kids, this story by artist and illustrator Ed Emberley is told with the help of clever die-cut pages that gradually reveal a monster with big, colorful shapes.

Technically an alphabet book, Once Upon an Alphabet is really a set of 26 clever stories about each letter. “My kids have laughed and loved this book for years, long after any other book about letters has left the rotation,” says Strategist contributor Youngna Park.

This animal-sticker book lets kids place animals in the correct habitats and match names to the correct animals.

Through midnight tonight, Babiators is taking up to 35 percent off select styles, including a very cute pair of heart-shaped sunnies.

Early Black Friday deals have already begun at Nordstrom with up to 35 percent off select items. The Dusted Cocoa colorway of these UGG slip-ons is marked down for both little and big kids.

It’s best to buy gloves on sale because they’re bound to be misplaced soon enough.

Pierced’s Black Friday sale has also started early with 25 percent off sitewide on the brand’s stud earrings, huggie hoops, charms, and more. Notably, the sale applies to monthly subscriptions as well.

Lots of toddler and baby clothes are 30 percent off at Abercrombie Kids. This festive Fair Isle sweater is perfect for holiday gatherings.

Another holiday-ready dress that comes in red tartan or a holly-berry print.

There are some cool shoes in Zara’s kids’ sale section, including these mesh barefoot sneakers that have an appealingly tactical look to them.

Or here’s a pair adorned with capybara charms.

These vibrant dual-tipped markers will work on a variety of surfaces, from wood to fabric to ceramic.

Novelty sticky notes make keeping track of deadlines and to-do lists much more fun.

This nostalgic French notebook will always be a classic.

Paint by numbers can help budding artists learn how to use a color to convey depth, light, and shadow. Writer Alexandra Lange recommends the sets she bought from Pop Shop America, which she worked on with her then-tween son.

Our best less-expensive baby carrier overall is durable, easy to wipe clean or machine wash, and looks expensive.

This is the floor-stand version of one of our favorite baby monitors.

Ali Brunson’s child can’t live without these stylish Lalo stacking cups. “Easy to clean, easy to dry,” she told us.

entry.title: What Constance Wu Can’t Live Without
entry.summary: “I order it in bulk, and I go through a jar a week.”
entry.content:
If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what everyday stuff famous people add to their carts — like mascara or a sleep mask. We asked actress Constance Wu — who stars in season two of The Terminal List, now streaming on Prime Video — about the all-purpose ointment, screen-free kids’ audio player, and flavorful chile topping she can’t live without.

It’s amazing. It’s so portable and easy. When your kids have an emergency or if you just think the public bathroom is too gross, you just unfold it, put the little bag in, they go, and then you toss the bag. I feel like it’s brought my anxiety levels down a lot because knowing I have it makes me not as worried about a potty emergency. My daughter is 6 now, so she doesn’t have to use it as much. But for my 3-year-old, it’s still good to have on hand.

You can use it on everything: diaper rash, eczema, scrapes or cuts. First you wash it with soap and water, of course, but then you put Aquaphor on top of it. I use it as a hand lotion sometimes or as lip balm. I have it all over my house, and I always have it with me. I have both the big tubs and the travel tubes. I keep the tubes in the pockets of multiple jackets and purses and bags. I also have a couple of the tubs in my house. It’s one thing I actually, truly think I can’t live without.

This is my favorite toy for kids. I don’t want to get in trouble with anybody, but I don’t like LEGOs. I ban them in my house because it hurts when you step on them. Magna-Tiles do not hurt when you step on them. My kids can play with them for endless amounts of time, and they clean up really nicely because they just stack into perfect cubes. Over the years, I’ve gotten many different sets. Some are themed, like they’ll have snowflakes on them or something, but the shape is still the same. Some of them come with little animals or cars. But the kids actually don’t play with the animals or the cars that much. They’ll put their regular, like, Paw Patrol figurines on the Magna-Tiles instead.

The Yoto player, oh my God. That you definitely can’t live without when you have screen-free kids, which I did for the longest time, literally until my daughter was 5 and a half. The Yoto player is kind of like an audiobook. It’s like a cube, and there’s no screens. It’s just somebody telling a story. My kids will stick a card in and listen to the story while they’re playing with their Barbies or Magna-Tiles, and they’re very content with that. It’s their own little portable speaker they can move around. I don’t feel bad about it because it’s not a dopamine hit the way a screen is. I think it actually just teaches them to listen and follow a story, and they really do. But you have to start with the Yoto. I feel like if you start with screens and then try to take them to the Yoto, they won’t get into it.

There’s also an app so you don’t have to take the player around with you. You play it on your phone, and if they have headphones, they can listen to it. I’ve done that on the subway. But actually, when I take my kids on the subway, I like for them to be okay sitting there without being stimulated. I’d like for them to be aware of their environment. They can hear what’s happening and look at what’s happening and be okay with that. So I don’t usually try to do things like that out of the house.

An all-time classic. I’ve tried all the fancy face washes; I’ve gone through phases where I’ve tried other things. When I lived in L.A., something about the L.A. air did something to my skin that was just not good, so while I was there, I had to use Clearasil, actually. But now that I’m back on the East Coast, I’m back to the Cetaphil. Cetaphil’s still the best one for me. I don’t have sensitive skin. My skin is very tough. But just in terms of how it makes my skin feel, I feel clean. I feel moisturized. I don’t feel like I have a bunch of crap on my face. I think it’s just a good all-around cleanser. I’m 44, and I’ve been using it since I was 18.

I get almost all my clothes on ThredUp now. It’s sustainable, and you can get very high-quality things for essentially free because what I do is I send in my old clothes. My old clothes get sold, and then you get credit in your ThredUp account that you can use to buy other stuff. I send in kids’ clothes, too, because kids grow out of stuff really quickly. Anything that they can’t sell, they recycle. So it’s an easy way to clear out your closet, and I love doing that frequently.

I shop based on material. I’ll just look for things that are made out of silk or wool or cashmere or things that are good quality. Based off of that, I get a lot of my basics. When I think about the fact that every year retailers and fashion brands come up with new lines of clothing, I’m like, This must produce so much waste. It’s hard for me to not think about that now when the things I get from ThredUp are perfectly fine — lovely, even.

Underwear is not something that you want to buy secondhand. I feel like Quince has really good, substantial underwear for kids. They say it’s organic, and I believe them. It fits my kids well, and it’s good quality — especially for my daughter because I think sometimes the underwear they make for girls is so flimsy. They last really well, long after the kids grow out of them.

Let me tell you, you can get the most amazing cashmere blankets from the fanciest places, but none of them are as soft and cozy as the cheap-ass fleece blankets you buy from CVS. You could find those kind of blankets at gas stations or Marshalls. My kids will always choose those cheap blankets over the really luxurious ones. Those blankets are just so soft — there’s something about the synthetic quality of them, maybe. It’s not wool. It’s not cotton. It’s, like, synthetic fleece. They’re so cheap, but some of them have lasted so long.

I love this stuff. I was over at a play date for one of my kids’ friends and that kid’s parents had it. I tried it and I was hooked. I order it in bulk, and I go through a jar a week. It’s crunchy and spicy and really flavorful. It’s just so yummy. I put it on rice. I put it on fish. I put it on kimchi. I’ve put it on mashed potatoes. I put it on hummus. I put it on salads — it’s really good on salads. And sometimes I’ll sprinkle a little on my hand and just eat it by itself.

I got this jacket over 20 years ago. I even remember where I got it — it was the Urban Outfitters that was on Sixth Avenue back when I was in New York in my early 20s. They had this thing called Urban Renewal, where they rework vintage items. I’ve had it for so long, and it works with almost everything. It’s wool and it’s warm enough that I could wear it on a cold day, but it’s light enough that I don’t get sweltering hot wearing it at a party. Even though it’s kind of an old-lady-looking jacket, there’s something about the cut and the way it hangs on me that looks very hip. I love that jacket.

It’s, like, a gray plaid material. On a taller person, it might be considered cropped, but on me, it hits right at my waist. It is double-breasted and has these little gold buttons. It’s kind of boxy, so it’s not fitted, and it looks like a modern version of what a cool grandma might wear. And it has three-quarter-length sleeves. That’s probably why it’s cool enough to not sweat in.

[Editor’s Note: Constance’s jacket is one of a kind, so we’ve linked to a jacket with a similar look.]

entry.title: The Best Advent Calendars This Year (So Far)
entry.summary: With Bonne Maman jams and Augustinus Bader’s vitamin-C serum.
entry.content:
The Advent-calendar elves are working overtime this holiday season. Many Advent calendars arrived early this year; some sold out even before Halloween, while others are selling out as Thanksgiving nears. That’s not to say there aren’t any good Advent calendars left. Just as the reader-favorite Anthropologie 24 Days of Beauty is gone, Advent calendars from Bonne Maman, Jo Malone, Aesop, and Fishwife remain. But if you want to have an Advent calendar before Advent (the fourth Sunday before Christmas), there’s no time for dillydallying. This is our ultimate guide to the best Advent calendars this year. I’ll be updating this guide in the next few weeks regularly — making sure everything’s still readily available and including new Advent calendars worth getting. If you’re looking for more of our holiday coverage, we have definitive guides to the best early beauty Advent calendars, Advent calendars for Gen Z, food Advent calendars, and Advent calendars for kids this year.

In 2014, Liberty beautified the tradition of the Advent calendar, “swapping out candy for a selection of its best-selling products,” explained beauty writer Tembe Denton-Hurst, noting that since then many other beauty retailers “quickly followed suit.” For 2026, 21 of the 29 products in Liberty’s calendar are full size, including a Sunday Riley CEO vitamin C serum and a Sisley Sisleya lotion (which retails for $185). There’s also a travel-size D.S. & Durga Debaser and Jones Road Miracle Balm.

There are 29 “grooming, skin-care, and fragrance heroes” in Liberty’s men’s calendar; the 14 full-size products include a Marvis Whitening Toothpaste, Paula’s Choice Ecotin Booster, and Philip Kingsley Flaky Itchy Scalp Shampoo, plus a travel-size Loewe Esencia Eau de Parfum and Grown Alchemist Skin Renewal.

It’s the best of Dermstore — at a great value. You’re getting deluxe samples of EltaMD’s UV Clear Blemish-Prone & Oil Balancing SPF 50 and SkinMedica HA5 Hydra Collagen Water Burst Moisturizer, a full-size iS Clinical GeneXC Serum, and a trial-size Barbara Sturm Face Cream (which starts at $75 for 20mL).

Exclusive to BlueRewards members (it’s easy to create an account) is Bluemercury’s 31 Days of Dazzle with Augustinus Bader eye patches, Slip silk scrunchies, a eucalyptus Nécessaire bodywash, and more for every single day in December.

Many “fancy” names at the Bloomingdale’s skin-care counter are in the department store’s 25 Days of Luxury Beauty Advent Calendar: Sisley, Le Mer, La Prairie, and Dr. Barbara Sturm. There’s a total of 27 products (valued at $1,252, apparently), like a Le Labo Santal 33, SK-II Skin Power Re-New Cream, and Shiseido Benefiance Wrinkle Smoothing Eye Cream.

Your replacement for Glossier You may be in Bloomingdale’s 12 Days of Luxury Fragrance set, which has perfume samples of Byredo’s Gypsy Water, Bond No. 9 Nomad, Van Cleef & Arpels’ Orchidée, and Creed’s Silver Mountain.

Ulta calls this year’s 25 Days of Beauty Advent Calendar its “biggest Advent calendar yet.” You’ll unbox a Tatcha Rice Wash, Moroccanoil’s Moroccanoil Treatment, Osea Malibu Undaria Algae Body Oil, and about-face Fractal Glitter Eye Paint.

Take it from me, a former Anthropologie employee: The company’s beauty Advent calendars sell out faster than you can say “Maeve.” This year’s Beauty Advent Calendars — in 24- and 12-day versions — are already sold out (for now). But Anthropologie’s Holiday in the City is still available. It’s a whiff of the holiday sprit with festive-scented candles — snowmint, mistletoe and moss, cranberry fizz, sugar plum and vanilla woods, and evergreen and embers — and a juniper-cedar room spray.

When senior writer Dominique Pariso sniffed her way through drugstore candles, Voluspa’s came out as the fanciest. In this selection of the brand’s votives is French Cade Lavender (a woodsy lavender that reminds Pariso of her grandfather’s aftershave), Goji Tarocco Orange, Moso Bamboo, Crushed Candy Cane, Foraged Wildberry, and Noble Fir Garland.

Pariso called Yankee Candle “the best bang for your buck” of the drugstore candles. Burn through classic Yankee Candle scents — Midsummer’s Night, Lemon Lavender, Christmas Cookie, and Macintosh — with this calendar. Compared with the standard Yankee Candle that’s 22 ounces, every Yankee Candle here is 1.3 ounces.

A tribute to “the home of the bath bomb,” the 29½ High Street Advent Calendar features “bath treats” available only during the holidays (Sugar Plum Fairy, candy cane, reindeer) and six exclusives (including a carrot bath bomb and a mini swirly sticky-dates bubble, plus other Lush customer favorites like Unicorn Horn, Luna’s Butterfly, and Sleepy).

Just like the 29½ High Street Advent Calendar, this includes products available only during the holidays (such as a s’mores shower gel and hot-chocolate and orange lip scrub) and ten “gift-exclusive treats” (Turmeric Latte Dusting Powder, Santa’s Favorite Body Spray, Golden Bear Bath Bomb). But you can keep the pamper hamper itself well after Christmas, as the copy says.

Our Gen-Z correspondent Bella Druckman says in her guide to the best Advent calendars for Gen Z that “Urban Outfitters’ calendar may as well have been designed by a high-schooler,” as it includes Starface pimple patches and a Billie Eilish perfume on the top of teens’ wish lists last year.

The 12 Days of Revolve — which, at $89, is one of the most affordable Advent calendars here — is back with a full-size Kosas Lip Pulse and Ilia Limitless Lash Mascara, plus a mini-size Summer Fridays Cloud Dew Moisturizer and Allies of Skin GF Serum.

Deluxe, “travel-ready” versions of Sunday Riley’s dermatologist-approved Good Genes and Beauty Hall of Famer C.E.O. vitamin C serum arrive inside the carry-on–themed 12 Days of Skincare.

Featuring Laneige’s Lip Sleeping Mask, which Yuna Zarai, Ty Hunter, Ashley Benson, and Keke Palmer can’t live without — alongside the company’s Water Sleeping Mask and Lip Glowy Balm.

This variety of Glow Recipe favorites includes a Watermelon Glow toner, which Farrah Moan convinced other drag queens to use, and the moisturizer version of Plum Plump (which our friends at the Cut say is “like a sheet mask in a bottle”).

Korres’s Greek Yoghurt Wide Awake Eye Gel keeps me from looking tired, and I’m happy to see it included here with the “best of 30 years of Korres,” like its Santorini grape body milk, basil-lemon shower gel, and mandarin-neroli hand cream. True to the brand’s heritage, the 24 boxes the products come in are decorated with a symbolic tama.

The ultimate Manicurist manicure — with nail polishes, a corrector pen, a base coat, a top coat, a cuticle remover, buffer, and a file (a total of 24 full-size products) — right at your fingertips.

Open three full-size products, three travel sizes, and 18 minis in Kiehl’s 24 Days of Joy — including a Midnight Recovery Concentrate that “works like a magic eraser overnight“; Creme de Corps, which Rachel Antonoff moisturizes with; and Ultra Facial Barrier–Hydrating Cleanser that keeps associate editor Jeremy Rellosa’s skin feeling refreshed.

At Beekman 1802’s Kindness Cafe, a barista goat carrying pastries and coffee leads you to a mint and eucalyptus whipped body lotion, pistachio-dark cherry hand cream, and honey and orange blossom soap.

For the Ruby Woo wearer, 24 Days of M.A.C Icons offers lipsticks, lip pencils, and eye shadows in the brand’s best-selling shades, including Spice and Oh, Baby.

Before committing yourself to a pricey, full-size Ginger Turmeric Cleansing Balm or Chebula Active Serum by True Botanicals (a favorite of Eva Mendes and Olivia Wilde — and maker of the oil that gave me shampoo-commercial shine), try the samples in the brand’s 12 Days of Decadent Delights.

“Every jewel-handled drawer” of Charlotte Tillbury’s Beauty Treasure Chest has either a full-size (six in all) or travel-size Charlotte Tilbury product — from the Airbrush Flawless setting spray in updates coordinator Najwa Jamal’s makeup bag to a Pillow Talk lipstick.

Modeled after Jo Malone’s London townhouse, it has the brand’s signatures — English pear and sweet pea, lime basil and mandarin, and wood sage and sea salt — in cologne, hand-cream, and body-cream forms.

Seasonal Jo Malone products like ginger biscuit, myrrh and tonka, and orange bitters, which “smells like a pomander — festive in a Victorian way, not a Hallmark way,” says our senior editor Ailbhe Malone, are in this year’s calendar. And on the 25th day, there’s a 30-ml.-size fragrance (tangerine and honey) — for comparison, the other samples are 9 ml., while a full-size is 100 ml.

Sample an Augustinus Bader formula every day of the 12 Days of Bader. Maybe the Cream, which former Cut beauty director Kathleen Hou referred to as “the secret to rich-person skin,” or the Vitamin C Serum (our editor Lauren Levy noticed her skin was more even-toned after using it for a few weeks) will become a permanent step in your routine.

Aesop describes its Valise as full of “sensorial discoveries.” It includes a hand-model-approved Resurrection Aromatique Hand Balm and Lucent Facial Concentrate that’s formulated with rose petals and niacinamide, which beauty columnist Rio Viera-Newton has called the ingredient “the Switzerland of skin care” as it works for nearly any skin type.

Coming in at a whopping $955 — the most expensive Advent calendar on our list (so far) — this has a combination of familiar Byredo scents like Mojave Ghost and Bibliothèque, with makeup (a Rouge à Lèvres in Liquide Vinyl Fantôme and Satin Earth Dust) and “objects for everyday use,” including a candle-wick trimmer and pocket mirror.

You don’t have to wait for the next day to open these Bonne Maman jams (including limited-edition caramel with salted butter, strawberry with Madagascar vanilla, and raspberry with dark chocolate), as our senior editor Jen Trolio’s family opens theirs in a single go to enjoy with her husband’s homemade bread.

It’s the perfect surprise for a chocolate lover: creations of milk, dark, and white chocolate with other flavors such as caramel, raspberry, passion fruit, praline, coconut, and even birthday cake.

The 25 original confections inside Dandelion’s calendar are made by 24 confectioners (who were chosen after a series of blind tastings). Each chocolate comes in an ornament box with Danish artist Lisa Grue’s illustrations, and there’s a storybook of Nordic folklore and a star decoration for your window (a Scandinavian tradition) included.

In Compartés’s “whimsical kingdom” — where there’s a dragon and a castle beyond snowy pines — there are chocolates in flavors of buttered croissant, eggnog crème brûlée, pistachio marzipan, and salted honeycomb.

There’s no place like the Vermont Country Store, where you can get these liqueur-filled chocolates with Rhum St. James, Gin Gibson, Poire Williams, Kirsch Cherry, and Cognac Bayet from Abtey.

Bissinger’s has been in the confectionery business since 1668. “Inspired by the heritage of the Bissinger’s boutique,” this year’s Advent calendar has a glaceed orange au chocolat and dark bouche de noel truffles.

Once upon a time, Tony’s Chocolonely was the next status Halloween candy. It has remained a Strategist favorite over the years. In the brand’s Countdown Calendar, you get an assortment of chocolates with nougat, caramel, and hazelnut.

This house includes 24 German lebkuchen (often compared to gingerbread): chocolate-orange stars, milk chocolate with a sour-cherry filling, and pfeffernuse.

Filled with traditional kekserln like sacher husarenkrapferl (a chocolate-covered almond-vanilla thumbprint cookie with apricot jam), it may be the closest thing to the Café Sabarsky reopening.

A Marriott collaboration with Laila Gohar (and illustrations by Joana Avillez) features Casa Bosques chocolates inspired by resort locations, such as almonds and Meyer lemons for San Francisco, and pistachios and raspberries for Munich.

Perhaps an upgrade to Swedish fish are these gummies in strawberry-pomegranate, strawberry-apple, melon, and watermelon.

Better than Twizzlers may be Lakrids by Bülow’s calendar, with two pieces of licorice confections (or the equivalent size) beyond every door — in flavors like milk chocolate, passion fruit, salted caramel, and the traditional salmiak.

Nearly every “candy food group” is represented in the 24 Days of Sweets by Dylan’s Candy Bar, including jelly rings, milk chocolate, and cotton candy.

Following the Swedish tradition of lördagsgodis, there are extra-generous-size surprises on the Saturdays of Sockerbit’s candy Advent calendar.

This Williams Sonoma exclusive contains many of founder Chuck Williams’s favorite ingredients: Edmond Fallot mustard, a Giusti raspberry condiment and balsamic vinegar, Médicis chocolate almonds, La Favorita pesto, and Fabbri Amarena cherries.

You could “spice up your life” with the help of Parisian spice distributor Le Comptoir Colonial’s Spice Advent Calendar for Williams Sonoma, with za’atar (thyme, sumac, sesame), paella seasoning (paprika, turmeric, caraway), and speculoos blend (cinnamon, nutmeg, clove, anise, ginger) included.

Williams Sonoma’s 12 Days of Cheese is for those who understand the nuances of Muenster and cheddar (or just Kraft singles). Each cheese is made by a family-operated creamery in Utah from the milk of a fourth-generation dairy and other ingredients like wildflower honey, organic bergamot, and cayenne pepper.

A real popcorn snob needs kernels of purple, red, and sweet baby blue and seasonings of dill pickle, white cheddar, and buttery jalapeño from “Indiana’s popcorn country.”

Only the finest ingredients for the home cook: a Sutter Buttes balsamic vinegar and wildflower honey, Jacobsen sea salt, Nielsen-Massey and Madagascar bourbon vanilla extract, with a Williams Sonoma dark-chocolate peppermint bark and brown-sugar bear.

All the best snacks Harry & David offers: a Royal Riviera pear, Moose Munch popcorn, Mesa Verde trail mix, and Scharffen Berger chocolate squares.

If you (tastefully) eat fish from a can, here’s Fishwife’s smoked Alaskan sockeye with Spanish extra-virgin olive oil, sardines with preserved lemon, and mussels with sweet pepper and chile.

Fly by Jing’s 12-day Advent calendar returns this year with more unlaunched sauces and discontinued blends. (It sold out on November 5 last year, according to the brand — you know what to do.)

A collaboration between Nespresso and Swarovski, the Vertuo and Original contain coffee pods (including decaffeinated roasts), plus each has almond and lemon-butter shortbread biscuits and a bonus tumbler.

Tea drinkers might appreciate Whittard’s Loose Leaf Advent Calendar, with lapsang souchong, silver needle, English rose, and jasmine dragon pearls to sip.

In the Palais des Thés’s constellation-filled sky are the Parisian company’s Grand Yunnan Impérial black tea, Genmaicha Yama green tea, and L’Herboriste N°52 infusion (with peppermint, anise, and lemon balm), plus other blends and herbal infusions.

Sample varietals — rosé, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc — from Total Wine’s Winery Direct line.

Stationery nerds: Papier’s 24-day Advent calendar and first-ever 12-day Advent calendar are here with roller-ball pens, fine liners, and highlighters for pen freaks and thank-you cards and sticky tabs for those who still hand-write everything.

Or there’s a separate Anthropologie and Papier collaboration with a shopping-list notepad, pencil case, and A7 notebooks.

entry.title: The 14 Very Best Winter Gloves and Mittens for Women
entry.summary: Whether you’re grabbing a ski pole or a G-train pole.
entry.content:
When I began writing and researching this guide four years ago, I’ll admit that I was the type of person who purchased a cheap pair of knit gloves at the start of every winter and simply hoped for the best. Those gloves developed holes quickly and riddled my text messages with typos despite supposedly being touchscreen-compatible. They were invariably discarded and left to languish at the bottom of various tote bags, never to be worn again. I’ve since found that investing in a sleeker and more dexterous pair of winter gloves makes life much easier during the colder months. Whether you’re walking to the subway, running around the park, or taking a selfie on a ski lift, the right pair will keep your hands cozy and comfortable without getting too sweaty or preventing you from swiping on your smartphone.

To find the best winter gloves and mittens for women, I talked to outdoor-gear experts and even professional snowboarders about their favorites. Then I tested their recommendations out for myself while also asking fellow Strategist staffers about how they keep their hands well insulated season after season. You’ll find recommendations here for windproof gloves to protect your knuckles while pushing a stroller, running gloves that’ll prevent your fingers from freezing while you select a new playlist, and hiking gloves you can keep on while you take photos of surrounding vistas. While you’re here, I’ve also written guides to the best winter parkas and boots for women.

Updated on November 9, 2026
I’ve updated our favorite women’s gloves with the latest pricing and availability and added gloves from Lands’ End, Hefstra, Arc’teryx, and Dakine to this list.

The material of the glove will tell you a lot about the best use case and the level of warmth you can expect. Leather, for example, is windproof but less effective in damp conditions. Polyester or fleece will dry quickly and let your fingers breathe, but that means it’s not the most windproof. For optimum protection against wind and water, including melted snow, I looked for gloves made with materials like nylon and Gore-Tex.

Two features make for a good pair of tech-friendly gloves. First, those all-important touchscreen-compatible fingertips, which conduct electricity and can therefore interact with your smartphone screen, enabling you to make calls, send messages, and take photos without going barehand. Some gloves feature five touchscreen fingertips, while others only enable you to use your thumbs and index fingers. The latter option is fine if you’re skipping songs on Spotify, but the former is preferable if you’re texting a lot.

Some gloves explicitly designed for exercising outdoors are made with silicone grips on the palms that’ll help you hold on to that precious phone when you’re on the move. While this is not an essential feature for everyone, I’ve noted which gloves are grippier than others.

I decided on three price points, denoted as $ (less than $20), $$ (less than $50), and $$$ (more than $50).

Material: Nylon and leather | Smartphone compatibility: Five fingers, palm grip | Price: $$

I purchased these gloves for the five-day W Trek in Patagonia’s Torres Del Paine National Park in 2022, and they’ve since become my default pair for both hiking and everyday use. I like that they’re thin enough to provide ample dexterity when fishing items out of a bag or taking photos with a smartphone camera, yet thick enough to insulate against frosty mornings or random rainstorms. The touchscreen fingertips are highly responsive, and stretchy cuffs prevent cold wrists while making it easy to take the gloves off with one hand. (The wrist cuffs clip together, too, which helps prevent the gloves from becoming orphaned from one another in my sock drawer or backpack.) Strategist associate editor Jeremy Rellosa has also owned a pair of these gloves for years and agrees that they’re ideal for biking, walking around town, and wearing on runs. Brian Githens, a certified ski instructor at the Jackson Hole Mountain Sports School, gives them two insulated thumbs up, adding that the gloves’ grippy suede palms are great for holding onto ski poles. While they’re warm enough for everyday winter wear in a city like New York, in extremely cold conditions I’d use these as liner gloves and pack an additional pair of mittens to put on top.

Material: Knit Polyester | Smartphone compatibility: Three fingers, palm grip | Price: $

I was initially skeptical about Achiou’s astoundingly affordable gloves, despite their thousands of glowing Amazon reviews. That’s because knit gloves tend to fit a little loosely, which inhibits touchscreen use and dexterity in general. But upon ordering a pair, I was surprised by how sleek they are; while such a low price implies disposability, in terms of comfort and fit, they are far superior to other cheap pairs that I’ve tried over the years, and the fleece lining means they’re also quite a lot warmer. Rubberized grippy palms make it easier to hold onto a smartphone or hiking pole or slippery handrail when descending the subway stairs, and elastic cuffs keep cold air out. As with the Black Diamond Screentaps, these are sleek enough to be worn as liner gloves underneath a bulkier pair of mittens. Note that sizing runs a little small.

Material: Acrylic, nylon, polyester | Smartphone compatibility: Five fingers, palm grip | Price: $$

As a heavy group-chat participant, I personally think that smartphone compatibility is the No. 1 most important winter-glove feature. And if you’re using your phone a lot outside and like the soft feel of knit gloves, it might be worth upgrading from the Achious above to these. They are woven with a conductive fiber on all five fingertips, as opposed to just three, and are also very grippy. The microfleece lining and dual-layer construction help keep the heat in, and the snug fit enhances dexterity. Travel journalist Brittany Loggins initially bought these gloves for their look and affordable price, and now she can’t go on trips without them.

Material: Recycled polyester fleece | Smartphone compatibility: Two fingers, palm grip | Price: $$

These gloves are made from the same fluffy fabric as Patagonia’s beloved fleeces, and they’re just as cozy. I first heard about them from Sleater Kinney’s Carrie Brownstein, who purchased them to conquer the elements in wintry Portland, Oregon, where she lives. “I needed a pair of gloves that were lightweight and that weren’t necessarily fashion gloves for going out,” she explains. “These don’t look like I’m going out to play in the snow either; they’re pretty versatile in terms of what I can wear them with. They’re very soft, and I can still use my fingers — I think that’s important with gloves, that you don’t feel clumsy when you’re wearing them.” She adds that the weight is perfect for an all-round glove and that the colors are cute but neutral.

Material: Leather and cashmere | Smartphone compatibility: Two fingers | Price: $$$

One of our favorite gifts to give during the colder months, these surprisingly affordable (even more so when they’re on sale, as they often are) 100 percent leather gloves with cashmere lining are ideal for everyday city wear. They’re sleek looking as well as smartphone compatible, which is unusual in a pair of leather gloves. When I tested a pair of these last winter, I found their thumb and forefinger touch pads weren’t the best for sending lots of texts (or taking multiple photos) compared to knit gloves with five-finger smartphone compatibility, but they certainly get the job done while also looking far more elegant. November is the month to buy, because they’re discounted for Black Friday and routinely sell out for the season by mid-December. (As was the case last year.)

Material: Leather, Primaloft, and brushed polyester | Smartphone compatibility: None | Price: $$$

Hefstra is the glove and mitten brand to know if you’re serious about leather quality. Its products are made from incredibly soft lambskin rather than the slightly stiffer cowhide that Lands’ End uses. They’re also cuffed and lined with synthetic insulation for an extra layer of protection against the elements. Strategist senior writer Dominique Pariso survived last year’s brutal, blizzard-prone New York City winter by wearing this pair of mittens and an alpaca-fur hat. “The leather is so nice, and they come in excellent colors,” she says. “They feel less dorky than a regular mitten while still being quite warm.”

Material: Merino wool and nylon | Smartphone compatibility: Two fingers | Price: $$

I love wearing naturally breathable and thermoregulating merino-wool base layers during winter, so it only made sense to test out gloves made from the same fiber. These Smartwool ones are my pick because they’re woven with a bit of nylon on the outside (it doesn’t touch the skin) for extra durability — they’d otherwise be too delicate for everyday use. They’re soft and slightly slinky enough to work as liner gloves but can also be worn on their own most of the time (during deep-freeze weather, pop a pair of mittens over the top). My journey with these gloves sadly ended when I left one of them in a diner; if you’re forgetful like me, consider getting a pair of gloves that clip together, like the Black Diamonds above, instead.

Material: Synthetic leather, Spandex, Neoprene | Smartphone compatibility: Two fingers | Price: $

For working in the cold, it’s important to look for a very well-insulated pair of gloves that still provide dexterity, as well as reinforced palms and fingertips to prevent wear and tear. Writer and film wrangler Maggie Slepian wears these gloves on winter film shoots in frigid Montana, where standard days on set can stretch for 12 hours while temperatures reach -15 degrees with cutting wind. She says they’re plenty warm, and the added palm grips make it easier to handle horses or perform other dexterous tasks. Elastic cuffs also make these gloves easier to slip on and off when needed, compared to those with a hook-and-loop fastening.

Material: Leather, Gore-Tex, polyester fleece | Smartphone compatibility: None | Price: $$$

When spending a lot of time outside in winter (whether you’re hiking or just committing to your daily walks in the park before work), it’s worth investing in a pair of thick, waterproof gloves to wear over the top of a thinner, more smartphone-compatible pair. Strategist senior writer Liza Corsillo recommends Arc’teryx’s Ventas for this purpose. She initially acquired them to keep her hands extra warm while pushing around a stroller, and they’ve since become permanent tools in her winter-survival arsenal. While bulkier than the pairs above, they’re not as heavy as ski gloves, which means they’re “great for protecting from cold wind and light enough to keep in my bag all the time,” she says.

Material: Polyester, Gore-Tex | Smartphone compatibility: Removable liner gloves with two-finger compatibility | Price: $$$

I’ve often been disappointed by ski gloves, many of which seem to develop finger holes quickly, fail to live up to their promised waterproofing, or get overly sweaty inside. When buying gloves for the slopes, the most important thing is that they have to be waterproof, windproof, and breathable, advises Liz Lamanna, manager and buyer at Brooklyn-based outdoor shop Panda Sport. “Just like in the gym, you want materials that will wick away sweat and are breathable so that you stay dry and warm,” she explains. Look for gloves labeled with Gore-Tex, the go-to material for waterproofing outdoor gear. Analisa Price, who works in apparel product management and writes the blog Femignarly, recommends these Dakine gloves (which come with smartphone-compatible liners) for beginner and intermediate skiers. She likes that they have zippered pockets for hand warmers, a wrist leash to prevent you from losing them, and wrist cinches to keep out snow. They also have a built-in thumb goggle squeegee to remove ice or snow from your lenses.

Material: Polyester, spandex | Smartphone compatibility: Two fingers | Price: $

For advice on what to wear when winter running, I turned to Strategist junior writer Brenley Goertzen, who is known to lace up her shoes in all seasons. She calls these lightweight and breathable gloves from Nike a lifesaver, because “the touchscreen feature allows me to change my music or hit buttons on my Garmin watch without stopping, so I can still be in full stride.” The slimmer silhouette means you won’t feel weighed down as you move, plus a fitted cuff retains heat balanced with the Dri-Fit technology’s breathability. Goertzen says that while these gloves aren’t waterproof, they are durable enough for contact with snow without adversely affecting touchscreen compatibility.

Material: Recycled polyester | Smartphone compatibility: Convertible mitten allows finger access | Price: $$

If you’re not so fussed about using your fingers to change songs while running, a pair of mittens will be warmer than gloves. Chelsea Rizzo and Allison Levy, the co-founders of Brooklyn-based outdoor-clothing brand Hikerkind, told me about these snuggly convertible ones, with a flip top and a secret pocket to stash a hand warmer on particularly frigid days. Should you need to use your hands to text or tie your shoelaces, it’s easy enough to briefly free your fingers for full dexterity. Rizzo calls the design “super functional and streamlined.”

Material: Polyester | Smartphone compatibility: None | Price: $$

If you’re doing intense outdoor work or just don’t want to have cold fingers ever, heated gloves are the best option. In addition to thick insulation, these have a AA-battery-powered heating element to keep you warm on the go. Journalist and lifelong Minnesotan Lindsay Guentzel (who has Raynaud’s disease, which often forces her to wear gloves even in the summer months) is “obsessed” with these ones from ActionHeat. “They have rechargeable batteries that you pop into each glove, and the heat lasts for five hours,” she says. “The trick is to buy extra sets of batteries so you’re constantly recharging the spare pairs.” She wears them while running and otherwise being active outside. (For a low-tech option, you can always invest in some chemical hand warmers — I’m partial to HotHands.)

Material: Waxed leather| Smartphone compatibility: None | Price: $$$

Mittens made from leather possess naturally insulating and moisture-regulating properties. They look smart, too, and will last for years. Slepian says these ones have been her ski mittens for many years, and they also come in handy on winter film shoots. They “start off somewhat stiff but start to break in after just a few wears,” she says, adding that she also enjoys their classic look, Thinsulate lining, and top-notch waterproofing.

entry.title: The 5 Very Best Toaster Ovens
entry.summary: Even better than your built-in.
entry.content:
Like their slotted counterparts, toaster ovens crisp up bread to golden brown, crunchy perfection. But as the name suggests, they also operate like ovens: baking, broiling, roasting, and reheating. While these are all functions your regular oven can perform, I’ve found that relegating them to a small countertop machine is faster, tidier, and doesn’t emit a ton of heat into the kitchen (a plus in the hotter months). I like them for making snacks (a quick-broiled piece of cheesy toast always hits), toasting nuts, warming up leftovers, and even baking small-batch foods (like a gratin in a smaller baking dish or a handful of cookies at a time). To find the very best ones, I tested several out myself — and talked to some professional cooks and recipe developers who rely on them, too (including a couple who even used ones as long-term stand-ins for their full-size ovens when circumstances required).

One note: This is a category where one brand, Breville, is an expert favorite (just like with espresso-makers). It makes three of the models on this list — but each with their own distinct advantages. Meanwhile, if you prefer a regular slotted toaster, you can find our guide to that, too.

Updated on November 9, 2026
We made sure all our favorite toaster ovens are still in stock and correctly priced.

Toaster ovens take up a fair amount of counter space, so here I’ve listed the dimensions of each.

All the toaster ovens on this list let you choose your preferred shade of toast, and all let you adjust the temperature and time if you’re using any of the functions. Otherwise, they have varying (though often overlapping) presets, so I’ve noted those.

Size: 18.5” x 16.25” x 11.25”  | Presets: Toast, bagel, bake, roast, broil, pizza, cookies, reheat, warm

This toaster oven is decidedly big (the second largest on this list). But in my own testing, I’ve found it to be an all-around great performer. It preheats in a matter of minutes, doesn’t make my whole space hot, and thanks to the stainless steel interior, is a breeze to clean. (Celia Lee, pastry chef at New York City’s NARO, expressed the same sentiment: Foods never stick to the tray or rack but if the inside needs a clean from crumbs, “it’s super easy to slide them out to put those parts through the dishwasher and wipe down the interior,” she says.)

The functionalities are intuitive to use: It has a dial to control temperature, another to control time, and a third to cycle through the different settings (bake, broil, and the like). Perhaps most impressively, it bakes, toasts, and broils super evenly, without hot spots.

For two years, recipe developer and newsletter author Caroline Chambers lived in a kitchen without a full-sized oven and had to use this in its place to create and test dishes. “It cooks things fast and efficiently,” she says. Jocelyn Delk Adams, a cookbook author and the recipe developer behind Grandbaby Cakes, notes the even heat distribution, too, which she says works just as well for making uniformly colored toast (like she does every morning) as it does for roasting a few salmon filets for dinner. She also likes it for reheating food, especially when she wants something to maintain its original crispiness, like fritters or pizza.

Size: 12.5” x 17.3” x 12.8” | Presets: Toast, roll, waffle, pizza, reheat, defrost

When I first got my hands on the compact and lightweight Panasonic, I was overwhelmed by its interface. Strategist senior writer Michael Zhao, who has owned one for a decade, put it well: “It’s a quirky device that feels like it speaks a different language than every other oven I’ve used — everything you’d expect to be a knob is a button. But once you learn it, it’s tempting to use it for just about everything.”

Indeed, he’s right. A look up close and a bit of playing with the settings, and it’s actually very simple to use. For toast specifically, you choose your level of darkness (the photo below shows the second to last setting, my preference). It also heats incredibly quickly, more than any other toaster oven I’ve tried. There are several presets (the frozen hash brown setting is admittedly a bit odd in its specificity, but it should work for defrosting anything around that size). And then there is temperature and time control, should you want to straight-up cook something. “I’ve done pork chops and bone-in chicken thighs, but it really shines for roasted vegetables,” Zhao says. “The lack of preheating means you can go from realizing you forgot to make a side dish to having perfectly roasted veggies before your weeknight pasta is finished cooking to al dente consistency.” One notable feature is the smart sensor, which automatically regulates the heat to maintain your desired degree and avoid burning the outside of foods before the inside is finished.

Strategist contributor Sarah Leon loves it, too. She’s had hers for more than five years, most notably during one when she renovated her kitchen and was left without a full-size oven. She says it was truly indispensable then for reheating leftovers and making both small meals and more elaborate dinners. But the pair say they also loved it before the remodel — and still love it after. “It allows you to put something in and walk away from it, knowing it won’t burn,” she says. And the size is yet another plus: “It’s very small, so it doesn’t take up much space. Still, she says it can fit a larger New York–style slice of pizza and a pre-made lasagna for two.

Size: 16” x 13.5” x 8.75” | Presets: Toast, bagel, pizza, reheat, cookies, roast, broil, bake

This Breville model has different mechanisms for adjusting time and temperature from our best overall pick (buttons instead of dials), as well as one less designated setting (there’s no “keep food warm” option). But the biggest difference — and one worthy of warranting its own spot on this list — is the size, which is about three inches smaller in height, depth, and width and just a bit over half the capacity. I grew up with this model and owned one for years myself before trading it for a slotted toaster a couple moves ago. It’s an efficient machine that perfectly toasts bread and uniformly broils bubbling cheese on top of open-faced sandwiches. The machine fits four slices of a standard square loaf and two of bigger sourdough — plenty of space for my needs. I like that you can set an exact temperature to bake at; I used it all the time to toast nuts and seeds, a task that feels a bit small to heat your full-sized oven for.

Zhao has also owned a Breville Mini since 2021. He appreciates that it fits anywhere you’d expect a toaster oven to fit (unlike the larger convecting smart oven, which can feel “surprisingly large out of the box,” he says). He mostly uses the “roast” and “bake” settings (it has plenty of space to make enough potatoes for four adults), as well as “toast.” “I particularly like the ‘a bit more’ button for adding extra color,” he says. “This is crucial because we keep our Ezekiel bread in the fridge, so even the darkest setting isn’t quite enough if there’s four slices in there.” His one small gripe is that he wishes the rack would automatically move out when he opens the door, but he gets around this by leaving a pair of steel buffet tongs on top.

Size: 14.1” x 12.6” x 8.2” | Presets: Sandwich bread, artisan bread, pizza, pastry, salamander

The original Balmuda toaster oven, made viral by influencer Emily Mariko’s videos, held a place on this list since I first tested the appliance several years ago. Despite its hefty price tag, it excelled at refreshing old pastries, leftovers (like a slice of pizza), and stale or refrigerated bread. While most standard toaster ovens can technically heat all those things, the steam oven does it better. To use that function, you fill the tiny provided cup with water and pour that into a small vent at the top of the machine. As it heats, the water turns to steam that imparts moisture to your food as it browns.

The Balmuda Pro, which debuted late last year, maintains this ability but has a new feature that I think makes it even better: a salamander, or superintense broiler setting. (For reference, the Pro retails for only $30 more than the first one. Still expensive, but at that point, worth it for the addition.)

The broiler quickly finishes dishes by browning, melting, toasting, or crisping the top — but it also makes it much easier to cook full meals, or components of full meals, than the original did. I’ve cooked chicken meatballs that turned evenly golden on the outside and many open-face cheese toasts. I’ve charred peppers for a dip and blistered green beans for a side dish.

I will note: The Pro is more compact than other toaster ovens on this list (by comparison, Breville’s Mini Smart Oven fits four pieces of toast, while this fits only two and requires an even smaller tray than a standard-size ⅛ sheet, like this one). It also allows for only three preset temperatures (350, 400, and 450 degrees). If your goal in buying a toaster oven is to cook full dinners — like to act as somewhat of a replacement oven — I would opt for a different model. But if you love the aesthetic of the Balmuda, often find yourself making food for just one, or cook singular components of meals for a couple of people, this does a good job.

Size: 20.5” x 21” x 12.5” | Presets: Toast, bagel, bake, roast, broil, pizza, cookies, proof, air fry, dehydrate, reheat, warm, slow cook

Food writer and editor Alyse Whitney has been using this Breville for the last four years (and used an older, similar model for eight years before that). It works as an air fryer, a countertop oven (Whitney says there’s truly nothing she makes in her regular oven that wouldn’t work in here), and a toaster. It’s big, so not everyone might have the counter space — but if you do, Whitney says she can’t recommend it enough, calling it her “ride-or-die appliance.”

She makes toast in it at least a few times a week and says her bread gets evenly browned when she tells the appliance there are two pieces inside instead of one so that it knows to heat a wider surface area. (It can, in fact, fit up to nine slices at a time.) There’s also a frozen button for bread straight from the freezer. The other functions get a lot of use, too. She uses the broiler for “instant cheese melting or to get the top of a dip browned a bubbly,” the reheat function for leftovers “without sacrificing texture,” the air fryer to circulate convection heat for crispy food (the fan isn’t loud, she says), and the pizza which ensures a frozen pie comes out “evenly golden” every time. entry.title: The Best Blenders for Those Low on Counter Space
entry.summary: Space-saving machines for smoothies, dips, dressings, and more.
entry.content:
While I own a magnificently powerful Vitamix, I rarely pull it out since I’ve started testing personal blenders. Unless you make smoothies for your whole family and big-batch dinners on the regular, or you rely on an extra-strong motor to create your own alt-milks and nut butters, a more compact model can do almost everything a large one can. Sometimes it can do it even better, like if you’re whipping up a dip or dressing that would get lost in a cavernous 64-ounce blending jar. Not to mention that personal blenders are generally significantly cheaper than full-size blenders.

To find the very best models out there, I consulted expert cooks and recipe developers about the ones they use in their everyday life. All the picks on this list are dishwasher safe, and all, except for two I’ve noted below, have 600-watt motors. I’m currently using our best overall pick and will be trying out even more going forward so I can compare them directly. And if you’re also in the market for a space-saving immersion blender, you can read my guide to those as well.

Updated on November 9, 2026
We’ve made sure all of our favorite personal blenders have been updated with the latest stock and availability.

I’ve listed the maximum capacity each blender jar holds. The numbers vary a decent amount here. The largest jar has a capacity of 32 ounces, helpful if you do heavier-duty cooking. The mid-size ones are around 19, perhaps a better pick if your main use will be daily smoothies you want to drink straight from the blending vessel. And the smallest of all is just six ounces, perfect for dressings, flavor-packed pastes, and more.

The depth, width, and height of each appliance will determine where you can store it, so I’ve listed each measurement.

I’ve described how each machine operates, whether you push and twist the jar down to blend or you press a button. I’ve also noted if there are any extra settings, like for smoothies.

Capacity: 32 oz. | Size: 12.01” x 7.72” x 15.94” | Power mechanism: Push down and twist

I have come to rely heavily on my Nutribullet Pro. Though it’s still much smaller than a full-size machine, it has the largest capacity of any personal blender on this list, meaning I can use it to whip up a salad dressing to keep in the fridge all week long, blend enough sauce to coat more than a full pound of pasta, and chop salsa for a generous bowl when friends come over. The two blending jars come with lids that turn them into storage containers, so I never have to decant into something separate if I’m saving the contents. The blades are powerful: I can throw parsley stems and whole cloves of garlic into a salsa verde and it blitzes them into oblivion. And the operating mechanisms are straightforward. I simply add all my ingredients to the jar, twist on the cap, attach that to the base, and press the whole thing down to blend. My hand acts as the power button, meaning I can easily pulse by pressing down and lifting up as needed. And the jar takes up hardly any space in my dishwasher.

This is also the model most of the pros I talked to recommend. “It’s powerful enough to get through a lot of the same stuff as a Vitamix,” says recipe developer and cookbook author Jess Damuck, who uses hers for dips, sauces, dressings, and smoothies. “I use it with a lot of frozen fruit, ice, and nuts, and it hasn’t had a problem.” Food writer and recipe developer Grace Elkus notes that she doesn’t even have to worry about making sure her mostly liquid ingredients are at the bottom. Usually, this helps ensure that everything blends smoothly, but Elkus says the Nutribullet can wade through anything. Former Strategist managing editor Kelsie Schrader has been making smoothies weekly in hers for over a year and says they get perfectly blended in less than a minute. “It hasn’t slowed down at all,” she says.

Capacity: 18 oz. and 12 oz. | Size: 4.5” x 4” x 11.8” | Power mechanism: Push down and twist

The cheaper Magic Bullet is made by the same company as the Nutribullet. While its 250-watt motor isn’t quite as powerful as the Nutribullet’s 600-watt one, it’s a solid machine that will get most basic blending jobs done. For comparison, it takes me a bit longer, by about 30 seconds or so, to blitz up tougher ingredients, like herbs for a smooth green sauce — and it feels like it’s working a bit harder to get there. But the machine is well-built. Its stature is incredibly similar to the Nutribullet, though overall smaller in size, which is a plus for storage. Though of course, this makes it tough to blend larger-batch sauces and smoothies, so keep that in mind.

Personal chef and recipe developer Jane Morgan, who has had hers for four years and says it’s still going strong, likes the 18-ounce jar for smoothies but prefers the smaller 12-ounce jar for emulsifying dressings because the blades have a lot of contact with the ingredients inside. She also uses it for prep work, like mincing garlic, making a mirepoix for Bolognese, or grating Parmesan. Strategist newsletter editor Ashley Wolfgang has been using a Magic Bullet nearly daily to make smoothies for the last decade (she replaced it recently with a new one, as it finally wore down). She primarily uses it for smoothies and says it “blends everything I throw in there super smoothly, including frozen fruits, in just about 30 to 45 seconds.”

Capacity: 18.6 oz. | Size: 5.39” x 5.39” x 14.06” | Power mechanism: Dial with smoothie setting

I very much like the full-size blender version of the Zwilling Enfinigy, so it’s no surprise its smaller-size model is just as great. I’ve made sauces, pesto, marinades, and dressings in it, all of which emulsify beautifully. This one works with a dial (as opposed to the press-down mechanism of the Nutribullet and Magic Bullet), and is also the only machine on this list that has a dedicated smoothie setting. The jar comes with a travel lid and — this is niche but worth mentioning — a vacuum-sealing lid that is compatible with Zwilling’s Fresh-and-Save system. (I have this latter setup, and I must say, it’s great for ensuring green sauces stay fresh and bright.)

Recipe developer Farideh Sadeghin is also a fan. She used to rely on her mini Cuisinart food processor, but in the year-plus she’s had the Zwilling, she has been turning to it more often for sauces and herb oils. “It does the same thing but with a lot more power,” she says. And whereas her Vitamix will take ingredients from full-form to super smooth in a matter of seconds, this is more likely to leave a bit of texture, which is a plus for pesto and certain marinades. Sadeghin appreciates the measurements on the side of the jar to help guide proportions, but otherwise says her favorite thing is that there aren’t too many bells and whistles. “It’s just easy to use,” she says.

Capacity: 21.5 oz. | Size: 4.13” x 4.13” x 13.43” | Power mechanism: Power button

The Beast is a particularly attractive blender. It has a cylindrical fluted jar and comes in quite a few pretty muted color tones (somehow it manages to escape the just-for-Instagram look of some other aesthetically minded kitchen products). Though its capacity is only second to the noticeably bigger Nutribullet, it’s quite compact overall — only slightly bigger than the Magic Bullet but smaller than the others on this list.

I recently tested one (specifically the Plus version, which comes with extra vessels), and was impressed by its power. When you press its sole button, it pulses. This is helpful when you want more of a chopped consistency, like with salsa or pesto. But if you hold the button down for a prolonged second, it will automatically blend for one minute. It winds down and then back up several times over the duration so as to let whatever is inside settle and therefore incorporate more evenly — helpful for smoother purées and sauces.

Elkus likes the Beast Mini Plus, too. While she does warn that it’s not quite as responsive as her Nutribullet when it comes to certain ingredients (sometimes she has to scrape down the sides in order for chunkier, harder ingredients like frozen fruit to reach the blades), “once it gets going, and everything is moving around, it’s great,” she says. “It’s never gritty.” Best of all are the accessories. “It doesn’t feel like the jar you just blended in. I would never even consider transferring this one,” she says. The jar also has a cap that you can stick a straw right into, if that’s your preference.

Capacity: 23.6 oz. | Size: 4.13” x 4.13” x 13.43” | Power mechanism: Power button

This year, Beast came out with a stainless-steel version of its blender. This is unusual, as small appliances made without plastic parts are few and far between. But the company is onto something, as not only does it give peace of mind, it works just as well as the original. I’ve used it make an ultrasmooth herb sauce (which took all of 40 seconds). I’ve pulsed a garlic marinade that ended up with consistent, not-too-big pieces of garlic — exactly what I was after. I’ve blended Sungold tomatoes into a fresh sauce. The blender can handle ice for smoothies, too, which you can then take on the go, thanks to the accompanying lid. Not only that, but because it’s stainless, your drink will stay cold for longer.

The biggest downside of an all-stainless blender is that you can’t see the consistency as you’re blending like you’d be able to with a clear plastic jar. But I don’t find that to be too much of an inconvenience. I simply start with about 30 seconds of blending, then take it off the base, unscrew the lid, and check inside.

Capacity: 64 ounces, 20-ounce jar | Size: 8.5” x 8.5” x 17.25”(with the full-sized blender jar), 5.5”

If you plan to stick to single-portion smoothies and small-batch sauces, one of the picks above will certainly save you money. But if you think you might appreciate having a machine that allows for bigger batches, it might be worth it to splurge on a full-size blender that offers compatible smaller jars. Many of them do, so it’s worth a look if you already own a given model, too. This was the case for Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang, who has been using our very favorite Vitamix since 2013 and didn’t want to buy an entirely separate small blender. She has a couple of caveats about the Vitamix Personal Cup Adapter: The cup is a bit bulky (though she does like that it’s double walled, which keeps her smoothies colder for longer), and the shape can make it challenging to get larger chunks of frozen ingredients to reach the blades, requiring her to coax the pieces in place with a chopstick or spatula. Using the adapter also takes a little getting used to. “But to be able to get the extra functionality from my Vitamix is worth the trouble to me,” she says. “And I also find the parts easy to clean; we just stick them in the dishwasher (they’re top-rack safe).”

entry.title: My Hunt for Heels That Don’t Hurt My High Arches
entry.summary: My ideal pair of heels would not require buying extra insoles or padding.
entry.content:
After a trip to Japan, where my feet burned even in my most comfortable sneakers, I saw a podiatrist and learned I have high arches, which makes standard shoes a literal pain to walk in because they weren’t built for me. If sneakers were painful, imagine how heels feel. A pair of orthopedic insoles and Hokas later, my feet are at ease on busy days out, but now they face a new dilemma: Orthopedic shoes aren’t cute. I searched for some kind of guide for a fashionable going-out pair for people with high arches, but the results led me to more sneakers or worse: orthopedic-looking heels that were frumpy at best. I couldn’t become another Gen-Zer doomed to wear sneakers to the bar, so I set out to find some actually nice-looking heels that my high arches could tolerate.

My ideal pair of heels would be comfortable on their own. They would not require that I buy extra insoles or padding, especially since I wanted to try slingbacks and heeled sandals without the risk of exposing my removable insoles or, worse, having them fly off my foot in the middle of the dance floor. The shoes have to intentionally offer arch support or padding in the design — so much so that I could visibly see it. I didn’t want to buy a pair that reviews say is comfortable, but that leaves me in pain after I wear them out. I’ve been burned too many times in the past.

Thankfully, all the pairs I tried for this story were more comfortable than any heels I already owned. Most pairs had relatively low heels — between 1 and 2 inches with the tallest pair being about 3.5 inches — and all were easy to walk in. Because all the shoes were generally comfortable, I ranked them by how long I could wear them before they started hurting my feet.

When I first began my hunt for heels with arch support, Reddit directed me to one of the only nice-looking suggestions I found, Naturalizer’s 27 Edit collection. These were the easiest to walk in at first, without needing much break-in time. But once I started wearing them out more, my feet could only last a few hours. When I went out to dinner with my fiancé in Calabasas, I couldn’t do my usual “walk around the block after dinner” routine without wanting to change shoes first. I ordered them in my regular size, 8, and they fit true to size. They go up to a size 12 and come in a wide width as well, making them one of the most size and width-inclusive options.

This pair also broke in pretty quickly. I wore these all day doing chores around the house, and I only took them off to try to turn off the fire alarm I accidentally set off while cooking. They have “PillowTech athletic-grade cushioning” that makes them super-comfortable — after walking on them on a different day for an afternoon running errands around town, my soles felt fine until about hour three, when I changed into Birkenstocks in my car to go into Ross. The style does run slightly big, so I would order half a size down. It doesn’t have visible arch support, but the cushioning was enough for a low-to-medium-steps walking day; it wasn’t comfortable enough for a full day out or a night that includes dancing or waiting for a drink at the bar, but would be great for a standard workday where there’s a mix of sitting and walking.

This pair had the least arch support built in; they have “inFORMA comfort technology” that adds cushion to pressure points on the foot, but I could still see a gap in the shoe with my high arches because the design didn’t have an arch lift. They were surprisingly easy to walk in for three-inch heels, though, despite not having a platform or real arch support. I did feel some arch soreness after a few hours of wear, so these would not be ones I’d wear for a night out with friends but would wear to Thanksgiving — where we take one nice picture and immediately take the heels off after. I ordered a half-size down, as my usual size 8 was too big to walk in comfortably.

These were my least favorite shoes, style-wise. That said, I’d seen a lot of positive reviews of this brand from other people with high arches, and I’m glad I gave this pair a shot. They were immediately comfortable, even with the thinner heel, and they broke in quickly because they’re made with a knit fabric instead of leather. I tested them out for happy-hour drinks with friends, and the walk from the parking lot to the restaurant was decently long. I felt immediate support in my arches, and the balls of my feet didn’t burn on the walk back to the car, something I’ve experienced with other heels in the same parking lot. It was also one of the only pairs my feet weren’t sweaty in by the end of the night. Unfortunately, this just isn’t my style, but it could definitely fit into my routine for work events where the chair-to-invited-people ratio is unclear.

These heels run true to size and were perfect for a dinner with co-workers that included a classic “I arrived here too early so we’re doing some window-shopping” walk. After going over a mile on concrete sidewalks and uneven thrift store tiled floors in Long Beach, the shoes were still very comfortable. Once we got settled at a dive bar, I didn’t dread getting up from my seat to order drinks, like I used to with non-supportive heels, because my feet didn’t hurt even after two hours of walking in them. By the end of the night, I forgot I was wearing heels and playfully did a little dance for my colleagues to show them the shoes were the real deal. These were also my first choice for a wedding at a ranch with an uphill walk, and I felt like I surpassed a new milestone as a heels newbie.

These Sarah Flint heels were the first pair I saw where I visibly gasped at how well you can see the arch support. The price point initially turned me off, but the arch support convinced me it might be better to invest in one solid pair than buy a bunch of uncomfortable shoes on sale. I wore them for a full night out to a journalism mixer that was outside in the backyard of a community center with uneven concrete floors. The night eventually shifted from business to party when my co-worker Savannah and I moved to our next stop: a karaoke bar to celebrate our other co-worker Bethy’s 21st anniversary with her husband, Colin. I didn’t feel pressure on the balls of my feet walking to and from the car, parked a few blocks from the bar. There is a bit of a break-in period, like with almost every heel, especially in the toe-box area with the pointed design, but once they were broken in, they felt like a pair of flats and gave me confidence to consider trying a higher pair from the brand in the future.

entry.title: The Boox Picco is the Tiny E-reader I’m Carrying With Me
entry.summary: But it’s great for that, too.
entry.content:
Tiny e-readers took BookTok by storm earlier this year. Gadgets like the XTeink X3 and X4 — which have magnets so you can attach them to the back of your phone — became a cheap way for people to carry all their books in their pocket without having to open an app on their phone and risk turning back to doomscrolling. But as popular as those models have been, their clunky software and (in some cases) reliance on proprietary charging and data cables and dongles made them less accessible to non-techy folks, and their basic software, clunky industrial design, and lack of bookstore access meant their overall reading experience just lacked the polish that made e-readers from more established brands attractive in the first place. So, when I heard Boox — maker of countless Android-powered e-readers and digital notebooks — was making its own card-size gadget, I had to try it out.

The aptly-named Picco — it’s just a tad larger than a credit card — is so small you don’t have any excuse not to take it with you and always be ready to get some reading done. It’s so light you barely notice it in your hand. But impressively small form factor aside, the Picco functions much like most other modern e-readers. The 3.97-inch display touchscreen is easy to navigate, it has a front light for easy reading in the dark, and you can load it with more books than you could read in a year.

While Boox isn’t the first company to pack all that into such a small form factor (that honor goes to XTeink with the X4 Pro), it’s the first to do so with so much style. The edges of the Picco are made of a soft-texture aluminum, while the plastic back features a nice dual-tone design. On the right side of the Picco, there’s a display/power button, as well as two buttons for turning the page. On the bottom-left corner is a single switch that lets you toggle the device’s front light without diving through menus as you must on most other e-readers.

Despite its small display, the Picco can fit enough text onscreen to provide a few minutes’ worth of reading — precisely what Boox says the reader is designed for — and with some fine-tuning, text can look just as good as on a Kindle or Kobo — albeit on a much smaller display.

Great as the Picco is as an e-reader, though, that’s not all Boox wants it to be known for. It’s the first in Boox’s new Tiles line of e-ink devices, which the company says are meant to be “lifestyle companions” with more capabilities than a typical reader. These devices don’t aspire to be full-service tablets, but in the Picco’s case, that means adding some light task-management abilities. There’s a barebones to-do app that lets you tick off tasks on the go, though you can’t create new tasks on the Picco. To do that, you’ll need to connect the device to your computer or use the company’s app while the Picco is connected to Wi-Fi. It’s a hassle compared to syncing your tasks across a phone, tablet, and computer, but I’ve enjoyed taking a few minutes every morning to input my most pressing tasks into the Picco and carrying it with me while I work. There’s also a Pomodoro timer app to help you stay on task for bursts of time, plus a countdown app. That’s a far cry from the functionality you can get out of Boox’s Android-powered devices that let you install third-party apps, but it’s also more than you can do with most tiny e-readers.

The Picco’s most noticeable exclusion is the lack of an e-book store. To get books onto the device, you’ll need to use DRM-free files in the EPUB format (though the Picco will convert them to a proprietary format), which is increasingly difficult as Amazon has made it impossible to download copies of the books you’ve purchased through its Kindle store. You can legally obtain free e-books through sources like Standard Ebooks, but that limits you to public-domain books. There’s also the option of buying e-books directly from publishers that offer them (I like Verso Books), but that’s not an option for every publisher so you may not be able to legally obtain a digital copy of the book you want.

It’s also worth knowing that while Boox advertises the Picco as supporting microSD cards up to two terabytes — enough space for more books than you could read in several lifetimes — it struggles with handling large libraries. I tested this by loading around 800 e-books onto the included 16 GB microSD card. They all transferred just fine, but the Picco’s software lets you see only 100 pages of e-books in the library view, and each page has room for only six books. That won’t be a problem if you have a library of under 600 books but may be important if you intend to make this your primary reading device.

And while the Picco’s display is quite readable, the preinstalled system font has some oddball kerning (in particular extra spacing between any apostrophe and letter, so words like “it’s” looked like “it’ s” and so on). That’s easily fixed by installing a custom font, but doing that requires finding a font that’s pleasant to your eyes, then jumping through some hoops. Once you have the font file you’d like to use on the Picco, you can install it using either Boox’s app or the company’s website. In either case, you’ll need an account. Both the app and the site have a page where you can import fonts, and it takes only a few taps (or clicks). Once that’s done, you can change the font in all your e-books. Beyond that, you can also customize the spacing of the lines and margins on each page, as well as the font’s weight, and a few other options.

I prefer compact e-readers like the XTeink X4 Pro or the phone-size Boox Palma to larger-screened readers like a Kindle or Kobo, as they’re easier to carry in your pocket so you can always have a book (or your whole to-be-read stack) with you. The Picco delivers beautifully on that front. Its hardware has the polish of much more expensive devices, its screen — with a little doing — makes text look great, and the custom software gives this tiny e-reader more functionality than its peers. It’s so lightweight I can carry it in my pocket everywhere and pull it out while I’m waiting for a friend to meet me at the bar. That alone has helped me get more reading done than if I just carried a Kindle in my bag — that’s well worth the Picco’s $100 price tag in my book.
