entry.title: Everyone’s Favorite Normatec Compression Boots Are Now Heated and Even Better
entry.summary: Here’s why the latest model is worth the upgrade and extra cost.
entry.content:
I’ve always been an endurance appreciator — from my time competing in collegiate track and cross-country to my new favorite sport of road cycling — and as our resident fitness writer, I spend a great deal of time researching and writing about the recovery space, including orbital massage guns, creatine, extra-firm foam rollers, heated back wraps, lymphatic-drainage leggings, and more. Compression boots are one of those unicorn products, meaning there’s really nothing else on the market that can offer the same experience on rest days. They’re meant to improve circulation and reduce muscle soreness by using pressure in a wavelike, sequential motion up your leg to clear metabolic waste and draw in fresh, oxygenated blood. While experts we’ve spoken to have noted that the performance results are mixed in regards to their ability to speed up general recovery, in the decade I’ve been using them, I’ve found that compression boots always make me feel less achy and stiff. Hyperice is still considered the most trusted (and most expensive) maker of compression boots, used by college and professional athletes and even athletes on the global stage.
​
In 2024, Hyperice released the Normatec Elite, a completely wireless air-compression recovery system with rechargeable batteries built onto the outside of each boot. While it was a very exciting upgrade at the time, I stuck with my older Normatec 3 Legs for practical reasons: While they require the tethered external air hoses and separate control box, they still offer a near-equivalent compression performance. But just last week, Hyperice leveled up its compression-boots line once again, and after testing the Normatec Elite Heat for over a month, I think the latest model is worth the upgrade and extra cost.

The most significant update is the addition of heat. You can choose from five levels ranging from 102 to 125 degrees. Using it really helps my lower-leg muscles to relax before exercise: In as little as ten minutes, any stiffness or tension has melted away. Thanks to flexible graphene sheets, all five chambers of the boots are covered with heat without any gaps. You can also choose from seven levels of dynamic air compression (40 to 110 mmHg). I’ve started using the heat and compression before working out, not just for recovery.

While the fully wireless design — both cordless and hoseless — is not new ( the Normatec Elite is also cord-free), this was my first time using this handy system, and it made the compression boots more convenient to use and store. Each boot has a control pack and compressor built in with buttons for adjusting the pressure, heat, cycle time (from 10 to 30 minutes), and zone boost (for focusing on a specific chamber of your leg during a session), plus a new deflate button on the side. The boots are also synchronized like the previous version, so both legs will receive the same massage for balance, no matter which control panel you choose to adjust. After the cycle is complete, the boots automatically deflate (or you can press the deflate button at any time), so they’re ready to be rolled up for storage. With the older Normatec 3 Legs, I had to put my full body weight on the boots for a few seconds to force them to deflate. The sturdy zippers and ripstop material make the Normatec Elite Heat feel more durable than previous models.

The battery life is pretty impressive, lasting one hour on the maximum heat and compression levels (the middle levels are plenty warm for me). And if I’m using only the compression feature (which I also never turn to the max level), then the battery can last for up to ten hours (and, of course, the boots can also be used while charging).

With the new heat technology, the price has increased by $400 from the previous model. It’s worth spending this much more because you’re getting a combination of seven air-compression levels and five heat levels that you won’t get with any other device. It has really been a game changer to pull these on at home before a chilly morning run or following a hard session at the gym.

entry.title: The 7 Very Best Alarm Clocks
entry.summary: It’s time to start waking up on the right side of the bed.
entry.content:
As convenient as it might be to use your phone as an alarm clock, standalone alarm clocks come with all kinds of features that can make waking up — or even going to sleep — a little less painful. Some have lights that simulate a gentle sunrise, while others can play bedtime stories or relaxing nature sounds to help you drift off. There are models that charge your phone overnight without taking up an extra spot on your power strip, others with accompanying apps that let you choose from dozens of alarm sounds (just like your phone!) or sync to smart lights, and even some that project the time onto your wall for easier viewing. A few even double as Bluetooth speakers.

The best-known newer brands in the space are Hatch and Loftie, with their feature-packed models, but you’ll still find a wide range of options from legacy electronics-makers Sharp and Braun. To find the best alarm clocks, I tested 12 models by setting each atop my nightstand and dresser for at least a couple nights, trying each feature and taking notes on how effective each was at waking me up. I also spoke with Strategist writers about their favorites.

Updated on November 6, 2026 
These are still the best alarm clocks, and I’ve confirmed that the prices are correct and they’re all still available.

Alarm clocks can be either digital or analog, meaning they’ll either display the digits of the actual time or they’ll have a clock face with hands indicating the time. Digital clocks may be easier for some people to read at a glance (especially first thing in the morning), but analog clocks may be less distracting for someone trying to fall asleep.

Displays with adjustable brightness allow you to see the time during the day but prevent the light from keeping you up at night when it’s time for bed.

Whether you prefer to set several alarms as an insurance measure, or want to share a clock with someone who wakes up at a different time than you, a clock with the ability to set multiple alarms will make things significantly easier.

Some clocks have adjustable lights that simulate sunrise to help you wake up, or speakers that can play soothing sounds or guided meditations to help you get ready for bed. Others, like Amazon’s Echo Dot and Google’s Nest Hub, plug into other services to expand their capabilities and let you control other devices and services with your voice.

Some people prefer to be roused with gentle tones, while others need a piercing siren to get them out of bed. I made sure to include both types on this list, as well as models with multiple sound options.

Clock type: Digital | Adjustable brightness: Yes | Multiple alarms: Yes (2) | Extra features: None | Sound options: None

For a basic alarm clock, Sharp’s AccuSet Jumbo impressed me with its thoughtful design, big display, and low price. You can adjust the brightness to three levels, and even the lowest setting can be seen in a well-lit room, but is still faint enough to not be disruptive at night. You can only set two alarms on this one, but it’s easy to do so, and changing them doesn’t take more than a minute or two.

You won’t be able to change the mildly sharp beeping of the alarm, but the sound works well without sounding too unpleasant first thing in the morning. On the back of this alarm, there’s a USB-A port you can use for charging your phone overnight. In 30 minutes, I was able to charge my iPhone 15 Pro Max from 54 percent up to 72 percent, which isn’t quite as much as you would get with fast charging, but that rate for overnight charging is fine.

You won’t get any of the features (like ambient noise, sunrise light, etc.) that come with smart clocks like the Loftie and Hatch Restore 3, but its simple setup and easy-to-see display make it an affordable and convenient option that had no trouble waking me up during my testing.

Clock type: Digital | Adjustable brightness: Yes | Multiple alarms: No | Smart features: None | Sound options: One

For a barebones model that looks good and is easy to set up, DreamSky’s large-screened alarm clock is tough to beat. Its LED light comes in nine color options, and its large, bright numbers are the easiest to read of any alarm clock I’ve tested. I tried out the model with orange lights, and even at its brightest setting (there are five options), it was never overwhelming, even in a completely dark room. 

Strategist editor Hilary Reid says she bought hers to reduce her overall screen time and that it’s been helpful in that pursuit. She likes that the clock’s numbers are big and easy to read — they’re significantly larger than the numbers on the Mesqool projector clock, and a bit bigger than the Sharp— but aren’t so vivid that they’ll keep you awake. “The numbers are orange, which I find to be less shockingly bright than red or blue numbers, and they are fully dimmable so I can keep them very low when I sleep and then turn them up to their brightest setting in the morning,” she says.

Like the Sharp, there’s a built-in USB-A port you can use to charge your phone overnight. It only comes with one beeping alarm, while the other clocks we recommend have multiple, so you’ll have to be okay with the beeps it emits. It’s not horrible but not particularly pleasant, either. I also wish that this clock had its controls on the top of the device like the Mesqool, rather than the back, for easier operation. The snooze button is conveniently placed on the top, but setting the time or adding an alarm is tricky when using the buttons on the back.

Clock type: Digital | Adjustable brightness: Yes | Multiple alarms: Yes | Smart features: App-controlled, ambient noise, sunrise light, guided meditations | Sound options: 14

I ended up using the Loftie far longer than the allotted testing time, thanks to how successful it was at waking me up. It combines a classic, understated LCD alarm clock lozenge-shaped design with a subtle light that can simulate a sunrise to ease you into the day. The light glows just enough to grab your attention as you wake up; it’s gentle, and adds a warm touch to the room, both in sunrise mode and when turned on manually from the buttons on the top. Using the app, you can have it light up and play a nice tune to let you know it’s time to wind down and get ready for bed, and another when it’s time to actually get in bed.

The Loftie’s display shows both the current time and, in much smaller, dimmer numerals, the time of the next alarm. It’ll also tell you when Bluetooth (which you can use to stream stuff from your phone or tablet) is enabled. The display is smaller than on other alarm clocks like the Sharp and Hatch, but I still didn’t have any trouble seeing it from across the room while in bed. The top of the Loftie has four buttons: snooze, two arrow buttons for navigating the menu, and the main button for selection or play/pause.

There are 14 alarm sounds to choose from, including jungle animals chirping alongside a flute and gentle, repetitive strikes of a gong. If you have a Loftie+ membership ($5/month, with a trial month for free), you can also play relaxing music to fall asleep to, listen to guided meditations, and get horoscope readings. They’re all nice add-ons, and I did find they helped my anxious mind wind down before dozing off, but the Loftie has plenty to offer without the subscription. You also don’t need to pay the subscription to use the Loftie like a Bluetooth speaker to stream podcasts or playlists from your phone. Unfortunately, the Bluetooth setting disables itself after a period of inactivity, so you’ll have to turn it back on from the device whenever you want to use it.

The accompanying app is surprisingly feature-packed for an alarm-clock app. You can add multiple alarms, each with different sounds from Loftie’s library, and adjust the brightness of the clock’s bottom light via an adjustable slider. You can also choose from 14 alarm sounds, all of which have pleasant tones, though if you need a sharper, more attention-grabbing sound to get you out of bed, these options probably won’t work. The app also supports multiple clocks, so you can control several devices from one phone.

The company also sells a Wi-Fi connected lamp, which is my new favorite lamp. It pairs with the clock to coordinate wakeup routines, like dimming your light before bed or using a soft light to help wake you up. Every time it lit up along with my alarm, I felt like I was waking up in a room pulled straight out of the brightly colored yet softly lit future of Spike Jonze’s Her. At $250, it’s rather expensive, and you can only control it from within Loftie’s app, but the light does look great. Rather than using a bulb, the entire base of the lamp lights up, and you can set it to one of over 30 color options, including solid colors and gradients. All of the color options are relaxing, never too intense, and can work for anything from providing some light for reading or just helping you wake up in the morning.

Clock type: Digital | Adjustable brightness: Yes | Multiple alarms: Yes | Smart features: App-controlled, ambient noise, sunrise light, guided meditations | Sound options: 14

While I like the Loftie’s design, the Hatch Restore 3 is my go-to alarm clock. I prefer its more subtle look and I like its sunrise light more — though the Loftie Lamp gives that model an edge if you’re willing to splurge on it. The Restore 3’s light is significantly brighter than the light on the Loftie and has a fabric cover to give it a soft glow. Unlike the Loftie’s single-color light, the Hatch has 18 possible colors, and they can all be changed from within the app. My room doesn’t get much light in the mornings, and the Hatch’s vibrant but not overbearing light serves as a gentle nudge to help wake me up. With the Restore 3, Hatch added a button to toggle the light directly from the device; with the Restore 2, you had to use the app to do this. 

Like the Loftie, the Restore 3 has 14 built-in alarm sounds to choose from; I prefer the soothing chords of “Joyful Morning.” You can even play white noise to fall asleep to. Unlike with the Loftie, some of these ambient tracks are available for free, though others are available only with a subscription ($5/month). That subscription also unlocks guided meditations and fun things like the series “i’ll scroll 4 u,” where a host narrates what they’re doing on their phone in every episode; it’s sort of like a podcast version of someone’s hushed internal monologue. In one episode they comment on the question prompts their Hinge suggestions have on their profiles, and in another the narrator talks us through their hunt for a new couch on Facebook Marketplace. On its own, the Restore 3 offers more than enough to help make sleep a little easier, but I’ll admit, I’ve enjoyed trying out some of Hatch’s subscription content, so it’s worth checking out at least for the free trial. That said, it’s still more limited than the Loftie, which doubles as a Bluetooth speaker so you can listen to your own podcasts or audiobooks before bed. Hatch still doesn’t offer that on its clocks.

Atop the Restore 3 are three buttons: a Pause button to toggle routines without using the app, an Unwind Swap button to rotate between the unwind routines Hatch lets you set up, and one that Hatch fittingly calls the Big Button. It’s used for starting your nightly bedtime routine and snoozing your alarm; it also works as a dial for adjusting the alarm’s volume. These buttons are all easier to distinguish and press than the ones on the Restore 2 or the Loftie given their different textures. The Pause button is flush with the rest of the clock’s top, while the Unwind Swap button is slightly concave, and the Big Button sits right on top of the surface.

One caveat: Only one user can control the Restore 3 from the app, so setting alarms for multiple people isn’t convenient. You can set multiple alarms, but they have to all be set up from the same smartphone.

Clock type: Digital | Adjustable brightness: Yes | Multiple alarms: Yes | Smart features: App-controlled, ambient noise, third-party app integration, smart home controls | Sound options: 20

I used to watch TV before bed, but since removing mine from my room last year, I’ve started relying on a tablet version of Google’s Nest Hub as a mini-TV, and it works well as an alarm I can control completely hands free. The Nest Hub, which I’ve had in my home for over a year, has a large display — basically a tablet —that can show everything from the weather to whatever playlist you have on its built-in speaker. At night, the display will automatically dim when you’re going to bed. The Hub can run multiple timers, and even show two onscreen at the same time. It also makes a pretty great digital picture frame.

Google Assistant is built right into the Nest Hub, which means that in addition to controlling all your on-device timers, alarms, and Google queries, you can also sync it to third-party smart home gear and services like Spotify or Netflix (I have mine set up to control my home alarm system and robot vacuum). All that’s done from Google’s Assistant app, but once you’ve done it for one Hub, it’ll be good to go with future devices as well.

Like nearly everything else you can do on the Nest Hub, you can set alarms with your voice, though you’ll have to use the touch screen to change the alarm wakeup sounds. There are 20 sounds to choose from, and they’re broken down into four categories (natural, light, medium, heavy), based on their tone and theme. They’re all nice to hear in the morning — I like the music-based ones — and I like that the options are broken down into their tones, rather than elements like the forest or ocean.

Since it’s meant to play music and videos too, the Nest Hub has a better speaker than the Loftie: It’s louder and clearer. You can sync it with your Spotify, Apple Music, or YouTube Music account to stream your favorite playlists or albums directly from the display, or even have it play a YouTube or Netflix video before bed. It doesn’t work as a Bluetooth speaker like the Loftie, but since the streaming functionality is all built in and doesn’t shut down on its own, it’s far more convenient.

Clock type: Analog | Adjustable brightness: No | Multiple alarms: No | Smart features: None | Sound options: 1

For those who prefer an analog clock, Braun’s can’t be beat. The BC22 is modeled on the brand’s discontinued AB 2, which was designed in 1984 by Dieter Rams. Rams’ clock designs are considered classics for a reason and have many fans.

Unlike every other clock we recommend, this one’s battery powered, though you’ll probably only have to replace it once per year at most. It only has one alarm and one alarm tone, which increases in volume until you shut it off. The quartz movement should be quiet enough that the ticking won’t keep you from dozing off.

You set the alarm manually on the back of the clock. On the right side of the Braun is a switch to disable the alarm. The clock’s face has a soft orange backlight that allows you to see it at night but won’t keep you awake, and the hands of the clock have illuminated tips for better visibility in the dark. Below the clock, there’s a green light that indicates when an alarm is active, which allows you to confirm at a glance whether you’ve set one or not.

Clock type: Digital | Adjustable brightness: Yes | Multiple alarms: Yes (2) | Smart features: None | Sound options: 1

If you need a way to look at the time without rolling over in bed, get a projection alarm clock. I’d almost given up on finding a good one — so many have projections that are too dim to be useful — but then I came across this one from Mesqool. It looks like a standard digital clock, and operates just like one, but on the right side of the display, there’s a tiny projector that’ll put a temporary clock right on your wall or ceiling. You can adjust the position of the projected time, as well as its orientation, but not its brightness. In dark rooms, the projection is quickly spottable without being excessively bright, so it won’t keep you up. Even during the day, the projected time is still visible in dimly lit rooms.

The numbers on the actual clock are slightly smaller than the display on the Dreamsky and on par with that of the Sharp Accuset but significantly thinner than both. The digits on the Mesqool are also tilted at an angle that’s not as pleasant to look at as the numbers on the Dreamsky. The Mesqool has an edge on actual operation, though: The buttons are on top of the display, so you can actually look at the clock while you’re adjusting the time or scheduling an alarm.

The alarm sound is quite similar to that of the Dreamsky, so while it’s not especially pleasant, it’s not grating or annoying, either.

entry.title: The Very Best Sunrise Alarm Clocks
entry.summary: “In the morning, you don’t want darkness — you want lots of light so your brain actually understands it’s time to get up.”
entry.content:
Light impacts the ticking of our internal clock — it tells our brain to be awake, while darkness signals that it’s time to sleep. That’s why screen time before bed can interfere with your sleep. “In the evenings, you want absence of light so your brain can release neurotransmitters that make you sleepy,” explains Dr. Mandana Mahmoudi, clinical director of sleep medicine at NYU Langone Health. “In the morning, you don’t want darkness — you want lots of light so your brain actually understands it’s time to get up.”

Light isn’t the only thing that affects our internal clock. “The main thing is what we’re doing on our screen,” explains Dr. Dianne Augelli, sleep-medicine expert at Weill Cornell Medicine and New York–Presbyterian. “There’s just so much on there, like TikTok, your work email — there’s so much generation from our phone that can cause anxiety or excitement and that can really interfere with our sleep.”

If you’re like me and trying to become a morning person, or if you sleep in a room that doesn’t have plenty of natural light, a sunrise alarm clock might help your sleep routine. “If you’re a night owl and you want to push back your body clock, you can use light therapy — including sunrise clocks — to advance your body clock,” Mahmoudi says. These clocks mimic the light from the sun, which can signal your body to awaken, and many models come with calming wake-up noises and audio tracks in lieu of jarring alarms. Some clocks also have features to help you fall asleep, like ambient noise and calming modes designed to replace screen time before it’s time to hit the sack.

To find the best sunrise alarm clocks, I tested several models and tapped our sleep and tech writers to get their testing notes on their favorites. The most popular brands in the space are Hatch, Lumie, Loftie, and Philips, but each model has a unique design and set of features.

Updated on November 6, 2026
All of these picks are still our favorites, and they’re all in stock.

The main feature of a sunrise alarm clock is a light that mimics the sunrise. Some models also allow you to adjust the temperature of the light.

Each clock has a different way of setting the alarm and programming the light, be it through buttons and a small LED display, with dials, or via an app.

A common accompanying feature of sunrise alarm clocks is the audio selection, from different wake-up tones to ambient noise to radio.

I’ll note if the clock pairs with an app and/or has Bluetooth compatibility.

Light features: Low-blue white, blue-enriched white, orange, red settings; auto dimming/shutoff; 15–90 min. sunrise/sunset duration | Interface: LED display, two dials, buttons | Sound options: 27 sleep/wake sounds | Smart features: Bluetooth compatible

The Bodyclock Luxe is my top recommendation because of its ease of use and high-quality design. While it‘s the most expensive single alarm clock on this list (not counting the Loftie clock-and-lamp combination), I think it’s well worth the extra cost. When it’s time to wind down, I don’t like fussing with my phone to set my alarm and ambient-noise presets — after all, one of the major benefits of a sunrise alarm clock is that it can keep you away from screens. The Bodyclock Luxe FM simplifies this whole process with its easy-to-use interface. Navigating between sound options and alarm settings reminds me of a car-stereo system with its dials and preset buttons. You can choose from 27 sleep-and-wake sounds, use Bluetooth to play music from your phone, or use the built-in FM radio (I like to wake up to NPR’s “Morning Edition”). The Lumie has a glass lamp cover that gives the LED bulb a soft glow even on its brightest setting. One thing you may want to consider is its size — it’s nine inches wide, eight inches tall, and five inches deep, so it’s generally more suitable for a nightstand rather than the top of a headboard.

Light features: Warm white, orange, and red settings; auto dimming/shutoff; 20, 30, or 45 min. sunrise/sunset duration | Interface: LED display, five buttons | Sound options: ten sleep/wake sounds | Smart features: None

If you like the general design of the Luxe FM but don’t need Bluetooth compatibility, FM radio, a larger selection of audio choices, or a nicer build, then the Bodyclock Glow 150 is a great alternative. The setup is simple: There’s a button to set up your nighttime routine, a button for your alarm, a settings button, and two volume buttons. It offers a warm glow for sunset and sunrise, and its smaller size (7.5 inches wide, six inches high, 4.7 inches deep) fits on my headboard. One of my favorite features is the tap function, which lets me snooze the alarm with a gentle touch on the plastic cover.

Light features: Sunrise and sunset features, 20 brightness settings, auto dimming/shutoff | Interface: Buttons on plastic cover, tap to snooze  | Sound options: Five wake-up sounds | Smart features: None

The SmartSleep light is a simple alarm clock with sunrise and sunset capabilities and a selection of five wake-up sounds. It’s not the most customizable clock (there’s no app or Bluetooth connectivity), but it does have an FM-radio setting and a large, bright light. Strategist sleep writer Amelia Jerden has tested the SmartSleep and likes its straightforward design, describing the light as “very vibe-y and warm” and not overly complicated to use (it’s all controlled through touchscreen buttons on the clockface itself, with one physical button on the side).

Light features: Dimmable bedside light, color customization, auto shutoff | Interface: LED light display behind fabric cover | Sound options: Dozens of ambient sounds, meditation tracks, soundscapes (more available with subscription to Hatch+) | Smart features: Bluetooth compatibility, Hatch app

With its massive audio selection and app that lets you fully customize a nighttime routine, the Hatch Restore 2 is more of a bedside sound machine and sleep companion than a sunrise alarm clock. It can glow brightly, but because its LED bulbs sit behind a fabric cover, it doesn’t shine as vividly as the other alarm clocks on this list. Using the Restore 2 requires a Wi-Fi connection and the Hatch app. There are lots of audio tracks and light/color settings to choose from (I found selecting from the various lists overwhelming at times), but if you prioritize customization and don’t need an ultrabright light to get up in the morning, the Hatch 2 is a great choice for you. It’s also shallow (less than three inches deep), so it won’t take up a lot of space on your bedside table, nightstand, or bed frame.

Jerden tested an older version of the Restore 2 and agrees that it’s a better choice for folks who like to dial in their settings. “It has a ton of different color and sound options that you can mix and match for the wake-up and bedtime routines, so it’s really good for customizing,” she says. “But the intensity of the light never wakes me up — I’m a very deep sleeper, and my bedroom gets a lot of natural light in the morning — so it’s really the alarm sound that wakes me up, rather than the light.”

Light features: Customizable color settings, auto shutoff (lamp); nightlight (clock) | Interface: LED display with three buttons and snooze button | Sound options: Large selection of sleep/wake sounds, ambient noise, meditation tracks, 33 preset light settings | Smart features: Bluetooth compatibility, Loftie app

This pick is the most expensive option on the list and consists of two separate products, meaning it takes up more space than the others, but it’s one of the nicest looking from a design standpoint. I’ve been testing the Loftie Clock for three years, and I credit it with changing my sleep routine. Previously, I had used my phone as an alarm and never liked how it jolted me awake (the default iPhone alarms are jarring), nor did I like having my phone by my bed, which would lead to my scrolling before sleep and immediately after waking up. But the Loftie has ambient noise, calming snooze and wake-up tones, and multiple forms of guided meditation (which I use frequently before bed), and those can help me wind down, as opposed to using my phone. Plus the clock’s interface and soothing nightlight are simple and aesthetically pleasing.

While the nightlight feature on the Loftie Clock alone doesn’t have the sunrise capabilities of the other alarm clocks on this list, pairing it with the nice-looking Loftie Lamp (sold separately) allows you to turn it into a sunrise-alarm-clock system. “Besides automatically turning on and gently increasing in intensity to wake you up, it can be set to turn on when it’s time to start your nighttime routine,” says Strategist tech writer Jordan McMahon. He uses the lamp as the primary light source in his bedroom and loves how the entire body of the lamp lights up and casts a pleasant glow.

Light features: Dimmable LED light, automatic dimming/shutoff | Interface: No buttons or screens, controlled by app and motion controls | Sound options: None | Smart features: Bluetooth compatibility, Casper app

While not technically an alarm clock, the Casper Glow Lights are a handy pair of smart lights that you can program — via the Casper app — to dim and turn on, and you can schedule them to wake you up in the morning just like the other devices on this list. For an audio alarm, you’ll need to use these in tandem with another device (your phone or another alarm clock) that you would set up separately.

Operating the lights is very interactive. Flip them upside down to turn on the warm, ambient light (I like to use them while I’m reading before bed). To dim or brighten the lights, you twist them (they don’t need to be on their charging base for this — any flat surface will work). At first, I was skeptical of the design — there are no buttons or screens — but after a night of using them, I fell in love with their simplicity and find them fun to use. Their portability means I can pick them up and use them as nightlights, and they auto-dim (which can be tweaked in the app) so I don’t have to worry about turning them off as I doze. I would recommend the Casper lights to folks who want to wake up to a bright, calming light but maybe paired with a phone alarm or some other audio alarm, which the Casper lights do not have.

entry.title: What Jaedyn Shaw Can’t Live Without
entry.summary: “It holds my hair down even with all the training, the sweating — it literally does not move.”
entry.content:
If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what everyday stuff famous people add to their carts — like mascara or a sleep mask. Ahead of the NWSL quarter-finals, we asked Gotham FC midfielder Jaedyn Shaw — who is an ambassador for e.l.f Cosmetics — about the flip-flops, seasoning sauce, and red-light headphones she can’t live without.

It’s actually so fire. It’s my go-to, especially when I have braids. It holds my hair down even with all the training, the sweating — like, playing games, in the sun, it literally does not move. I’ve probably gone through six of those little containers.

It’s very similar to soy sauce; it’s just a slightly different taste. I put it on everything; it’s like the only thing in my cabinet that gets used frequently. I’m not a huge cooker, but it makes everything taste good. I put it over rice, I put it on my eggs — I don’t even really salt my eggs, I just put the Maggi on there — I put it in sauces. It makes everything better. They need to make little minis that I can put in my purse. My aunt always had the big bottle, and my cousins and I would throw down on the Maggi.

I never take it off except for during games and training. Jade is good luck in Asian culture. My mom gave it to me — she got one from her mom, so she wanted to make sure that I had one too. It’s jade and gold, and I’m also a gold girlie, so it fits with everything I wear. It’s something our family really likes and it’s comforting to have, the mixture of my family and my faith and the jade.

[Editor’s note: Jaedyn’s exact necklace is a one-off custom item, but we’ve included a similar one here.]

She’s all scratched up, but I love her. I’ve been wearing the Oura for a couple years now. I like how it tracks my menstrual cycle, how it tells me what days I’m in, and how it helps me with on-the-field stuff like knowing how hard to push myself, or what to eat and how to fuel myself — whether that’s anti-inflammatories or more protein depending on what phase I’m in. And then it shows my readiness, my heart-rate variability, and how I rested and recovered during my sleep, which helps me know how much I can push myself the next day.

I was really into the flip-flops this summer. Normally I’m like, toes are covered, socks on, I’m in sneakers, but I feel like this year was really a flip-flop summer, it was really trendy this year. And I had the worst mini sock-tan line, so I was trying to get rid of that. I also feel like the physios tell us it’s good to walk barefoot, but I don’t want to walk barefoot! So I’ll wear flat flip-flops, and maybe that helps. Apparently, walking barefoot helps your foot muscles.

I have three different pairs. One that’s very Brazil colors; I got those from a former teammate, Gabby Portillo. She brought them back from Brazil when she went to camp once. Then my other two pairs, I have a beige pair and a navy pair that I actually got in Brazil this summer, and they have a bunch of charms on them. When you buy them, you pick your charms and they punch a hole in the strap and press them in there — it’s like getting your ears pierced. And they’re so cheap over there.

I have them in beige. I feel like the noise canceling is so perfect, especially on planes. With traveling so much — there’s babies crying, the airplane is loud, like, sometimes I turn them on and don’t even play anything and just chill. It sounds kind of psychotic to say that, but it’s kind of nice. And then on game day, I listen to a lot of GloRilla and BossMan Dlow, very ratchet.

I red-light all the time to make sure this skin don’t crack. Obviously I’m young, but I feel like I have to start early. Dark spots, I had pretty bad acne — that’s a time in my life that we’re just going to leave — but especially with how much we sweat, and how much we’re in the sun, the red light helps soothe my skin, and I want the anti-aging properties happening. I use the TheraFace mask every night, in the bed, after my shower when I’m on my doomscroll. Sometimes I read, but most of the time it’s a doomscroll. I like that I can actually see with the mask on — it’s not super uncomfortable to have my eyes open. I go through the preset cycles.

I feel like I’ve been using it for a couple years now, even before partnering with e.l.f. Obviously the name — it grips — but even during games, my makeup literally sticks to it. I’m giving it a hard task with playing, I sweat a lot, but my makeup still stays. It’s at a nice price point, too, for how well it works. I do my skin care, then put the primer over that, let it sit for a minute or so, then I put on foundation or whatever other makeup I’m gonna wear.

entry.title: Iced Coffee and Skin-Care Hauls: The Best Advent Calendars for Gen Z (So Far)
entry.summary: Including one with enough Red Bull to get through finals season.
entry.content:
Gen Z might have it best when it comes to Advent calendars. They’re not quite kids and not quite adults, so there’s nothing stopping them from opening 24 days’ worth of coloring books or 12 days’ worth of “cheeky” Pink panties other than their wallet. (But, really, who’s to stop Gen-Xers from doing the same?) We’re still a ways away from actual Advent, but it feels like all the Advent calendars a Gen-Zer could want — from those filled with TikTok-famous beauty products to another with enough Red Bull to get through finals season — have already been available for weeks. I’ve been keeping track of each and every Advent calendar teens and young adults might want, and I’d recommend acting fast before they sell out. If you’re looking to peruse even more Advent calendar content, we have a big guide to all of this year’s best Advent calendars, along with dedicated guides to the best early beauty Advent calendars, food Advent calendars, fashion and jewelry Advent calendars, and Advent calendars for kids.

Update on November 5, 2026
﻿I added several Advent calendars, including new ones from Victoria’s Secret and Nespresso, and checked the price and availability of the others here.

Most of the beauty Advent calendars I’ve seen have at least a couple Gen-Z-loved beauty products, but Urban Outfitters’ calendar may as well have been designed by a high-schooler. There are Starface pimple patches (yes, the ones Gen Z wears out and about) and a travel-size bodywash from Sol de Janeiro. I also spotted a mini-version of the Billie Eilish perfume that topped wish lists last year.

The Sephora Advent calendar has been sold out for a couple weeks, but Ulta’s is still going strong. Inside, there are mini-versions of lots of viral products, including Sacheu’s lip-liner stain, some Benetint, and a pack of those buzzy Kardashian gummies (these ones are geared toward better digestion).

Revolve’s 25-day Advent calendar has fallen, but the 12-day version is still available. I’d say this one’s for the TikTok girlies — and, rest assured, there are full-size products inside. Ilia mascara or Sacheu eye shadow, anyone?

It’s the first year that Ipsy’s 25-day Advent calendar is available to everyone (rather than just those who have a subscription), and it’s full of mini and full-size products. The company has only revealed six items so far, but I spotted several full-size Gen-Z favorites: Gisou lip oil, Glow Recipe drops, and a tube of Too Faced Better Than Sex mascara.

When I interviewed shoppers at American Dream earlier this year, many teens told me they now preferred Alo over Lululemon. There’s a seven-day Advent calendar for those who agree that includes several of the brand’s wellness products and the claw clip on every girl’s wish list.

I’ve long said Dedcool’s nice-smelling detergent would make a nice gift for a college student, and the brand’s Advent calendar includes a travel-size version of the detergent that would be perfect for spring break. There are also some other purse-friendly staples — notably, a coconut lip balm and solid fragrance in one of the brand’s signature gourmand scents, Mochi Milk.

Laneige’s Advent calendar is a lip lover’s dream. There are no fewer than six lip products inside — that would be two lip serums, two lip glowy balms, and one lip sleeping mask.

Speaking of lip lovers — this one is dedicated to all things lips, and the Advent calendar itself is in the shape of a tube of lipstick. I think the Benetint, Make Up For Ever liner, and Kylie Cosmetics gloss would make for a nice lip combo.

It’s somewhat of a Gen-Z ritual to use a face mask at least once a week. Here’s an Advent calendar with ten masks and a couple of eye patches. Some are meant for soothing, while others target pore control or moisture, so you can bank them for 2027 or use them throughout the holiday season.

It’s been a few years since teens raided Sephora displays in search of Glow Recipe Dew Drops (and Drunk Elephant, too), but Gen Z still loves the brand. The 12-day calendar includes those famous drops in their original form and a tinted version.

E.l.f. regularly comes up during my conversations with teens, and its 24-day Advent calendar would make a nice gift for a teen who’s loyal to the brand. It includes some tried-and-true favorites, such as the daily cleanser and lip oil, along with two Advent calendar exclusives.

We’ve been experiencing a Victoria’s Secret renaissance as of late. The silk pajamas were a holiday hit with teens last year, and when I interviewed teens about their fragrance wish lists last month, they all wanted Victoria’s Secret fragrance mists and perfumes. This Advent calendar has a mix of both. Expect appearances from several Bombshell perfumes and mists along with some fun exclusives (a key chain and ornament, included).

We’re living amid the super dupes, and Dossier is a Gen-Z favorite for fragrance. The brand’s 12-day Advent calendar includes scents “inspired by” Le Labo’s Santal 33 and Tom Ford’s Vanilla Sex. There are some Dossier originals too.

Believe it or not Target, of all places, is where many teens go to discover new fragrances these days. The newly released scent-filled Advent calendar has several favorites, including the Athena Club body mist in Golden Vanilla and Eos’ body lotion in Fresh and Cozy.

ICYMI: Gen Z is still obsessed with all things Snoopy. With milk-chocolate toffee crunch and dark-chocolate mint squares, this chocolate Advent calendar is a step up from the no-frills ones from the grocery store.

There’s another Snoopy-forward one from Sugarfina. My boyfriend and I got the non-Snoopy version last year and loved trying all the different gummies. (My favorites, the passion fruit gummies and sweet-and-sour hearts, are in this one too.)

For those who have waited on line at BonBon, may I suggest an Advent calendar dedicated to Swedish candy from Sockerbit. It includes extra surprises on Saturdays (meaning bigger baggies stuffed with gummies). That should be the new standard.

I’ve made it somewhat of a tradition to watch as many dorm-tour videos as I can every August, and each year it feels like college students stuff their mini-fridges with more energy drinks than the last. I’ve only spotted this one from Red Bull so far, but I’d suggest Celsius and Alani Nu get on it, too.

Though if you’d prefer your caffeine in coffee form, there’s this one from Cometeer that’s filled with flash-frozen coffee. You can enjoy it hot or, well, iced for anyone who wants to bring iced coffee to their job interview …

For college kids who have a Nespresso machine in their dorm, there’s a Nespresso Advent calendar too (done in collaboration with none other than Swarovski). Each door has a new coffee pod, and there’s a branded tumbler at the end.

In New York pop-up history, Fishwife’s has felt as popular among my contemporaries as the ones by Parke and Pleasing. For those who couldn’t make it (and those who simply like tinned fish), the brand made an Advent calendar with its signature playful packaging. Inside, there are the usuals — smoked salmon, albacore tuna, and mussels — along with some fun mementos, like chocolate sardines and the company’s new collaboration with Bag Balm.

Fly by Jing makes some of my favorite fancy instant noodles (the other is from Momofuku), and its Advent calendar includes all the noodle flavors along with other spicy specialties.

For those who have made stationery the fixation of their 20s, Papier’s 12- and 24-day Advent calendars have all the fixings — roller-ball pens, highlighters, and thank-you cards included.

There’s also an embroidery Advent calendar for the 20-somethings who have picked up the hobby. Each day you embroider a new icon onto the calendar, which you can display at the end of the month.

I’ve been seeing Coco Wyo’s coloring books on lots of teen wish lists this year. Here’s an Advent calendar filled with 24 mini-versions of its coloring books.

If I were Snoopy, I’d be worried about Miffy stealing my fans. For those who have converted, there’s a 12-day Advent calendar filled with sticker sheets dedicated to the beloved bunny.

Pink is one of the latest additions to Tween Row, and I imagine the brand’s pantie Advent calendar will be a big hit with teens this year. It includes 12 limited-edition panties with festive bedazzled slogans like “Naughty” and “Nice.”

Victoria’s Secret made a slightly skimpier 12 Days of Thongs. Expect lots of bedazzled panties and lacy thongs.

Kendra Scott is still a top jewelry brand for teens and tweens (though Enewton is up there too). The brand’s 2026 Advent calendar has several viral products — including a couple of those pendant necklaces — available in either silver or gold, depending on your preference.

Between the brand’s pajamas and sweatshirts, teens can’t get enough of Skims. I’d expect the Advent calendar to go quickly; it has several fun accessories, like satin scrunchies, a faux-fur compact mirror, and a Skims squishy.

For our Swifties, I found an Advent calendar that comes with charms, beads, and chains to build their own bracelets.

Teen-loved mall brand Altar’d State has also made a charm bracelet Advent calendar. It has a gold-tone paper-clip chain and 12 mini-charms to put on it.

In case you were wondering: You’ll only find ankle socks in this Advent calendar.

Kitsch’s Advent calendar doesn’t include the viral zigzag headbands, but there are plenty of other festive hair accessories inside, like a cocoa-colored Cloud claw clip, pistachio-scented hair perfume, and white-as-snow satin pillowcase.

For about half the price of the Kitsch calendar, Conair’s has several clips and hair ties, too. The travel brush with a becharmed chain is also a fun touch.
